m1-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Install Python 3.11 or newer, VS Code, and Microsoft's Python extension.
  • Create a virtual environment for the course and activate it.
  • Install FastAPI with python -m pip install "fastapi[standard]" and say what came with it.
  • Check that curl works, and fix the install problems that stop most people.

By the end of the next lesson, your laptop will be a web server. You'll type one command, open a URL, and get back JSON that your own Python function produced. Every app you use works this way underneath: your phone asks a server for data, and a function on that server answers.

Getting there takes four installs, and each one does a different job. Knowing which piece does what is the difference between fixing a setup error in a minute and staring at it for an hour.

#Five pieces, one request

  • Python runs everything. FastAPI needs 3.11 or newer.
  • FastAPI is a library. It decides which of your functions handles each URL, checks the incoming data, and turns your return value into JSON.
  • Uvicorn is the web server. It listens on a network port, receives raw HTTP, and hands it to FastAPI. It installs together with FastAPI.
  • curl is a command-line client. It sends a request and prints exactly what came back, headers and all, which a browser hides from you.
  • VS Code is where you write code. Its Python extension lets it run files, pick the right Python, and debug.

#Step 1: Install Python 3.11 or newer

If you already have Python, check the version first with python --version (Windows) or python3 --version (macOS, Linux). Anything from 3.11 up is fine, so skip to Step 2.

Windows

  1. Go to python.org/downloads (opens in a new tab) and download the Python install manager. (It's also in the Microsoft Store as Python Install Manager; the two are the same.)
  2. Open the file and choose Install.
  3. Open PowerShell from the Start menu and ask the manager for the newest Python:
  1. Close PowerShell, open a new window, and check:

macOS

  1. Download the macOS installer from python.org/downloads (opens in a new tab) and run the .pkg with its default options.
  2. Open Terminal (Cmd+Space, then type Terminal) and check:

macOS has no plain python command. Use python3 until your virtual environment is active.

Chromebook / Linux

  1. On a Chromebook, open Settings › About ChromeOS › Developers and select Set up next to Linux development environment. A Terminal window opens when it's ready.
  2. In that Terminal (or on Debian or Ubuntu Linux), install Python, its venv module, pip, and curl:

If the version is below 3.11, your Linux is old; ask whoever manages the computer, or use GitHub Codespaces in the browser.

#Step 2: Install VS Code and the Python extension

Download VS Code from code.visualstudio.com (opens in a new tab) and install it with the default options. On a Chromebook or Linux, download the .deb that matches what dpkg --print-architecture prints (amd64 means x64, arm64 means ARM64), move it into Linux files on a Chromebook, and install it from the Terminal with sudo apt install ./code_*.deb. Then open the Extensions view with Ctrl+Shift+X (Cmd+Shift+X on a Mac), search for Python, and install the one published by Microsoft.

#Step 3: Make the course folder and its virtual environment

A virtual environment is a private copy of Python that lives inside one project folder. Packages you install while it's active go into that folder, so this course's FastAPI never clashes with anything else on your computer.

In VS Code, choose File › Open Folder…, create a new folder named backend-course, and open it. Then open a terminal with Terminal › New Terminal and create the environment:

Windows

macOS

Chromebook / Linux

Your prompt now starts with (.venv). If VS Code offers to use the new environment for this workspace, say Yes. From here on, python means the environment's Python on every system, macOS included.

#Step 4: Install FastAPI

With (.venv) showing, run:

The [standard] part is an extra: it asks pip for FastAPI plus the tools you'd want anyway. That includes Uvicorn, the fastapi command, and httpx, which FastAPI's TestClient uses to send requests in tests. Starting the command with python -m makes pip install into the Python you just activated, not some other one.

Now check that the fastapi command exists:

It prints a line like FastAPI CLI version: 0.0.x. The exact number will be newer than anything printed on this page.

#Step 5: Check curl

curl comes with Windows 10 and 11, macOS, and the Linux install above. Check it:

Windows

Type curl.exe, not curl. In Windows PowerShell, plain curl is a nickname for a different command, Invoke-WebRequest, which prints its results in another format.

macOS

Chromebook / Linux

The first line names the version, for example curl 8.7.1. Any version from the last few years works.

#Step 6: Prove it all fits together

Create check_setup.py in backend-course and run it with the play button at the top right of the editor:

This output came from the computer that built this page. It isn't inside a virtual environment, so it says False. On yours, the second line should say True and all four packages should show a version. importlib.metadata.version() asks the running Python which version of a package it can see, so a MISSING here means VS Code is running a different Python than the one you installed into.

🧪 Try it yourself

Click the Python version in the bottom-right corner of VS Code. The list that opens shows every Python VS Code found. The one marked with .venv is the one you want selected.

#When it doesn't work

⚠️ `zsh: no matches found: fastapi[standard]`

On macOS (and zsh on Linux), square brackets mean "match file names", so the shell rejects the command before pip ever sees it. Put the package name in quotes, exactly as shown: python -m pip install "fastapi[standard]".

⚠️ Windows: `Activate.ps1 cannot be loaded because running scripts is disabled on this system`

PowerShell blocks scripts by default. Allow scripts you create yourself by running this once, then activate again:

⚠️ `fastapi: command not found` or `'fastapi' is not recognized`

The environment isn't active in this terminal, so the shell can't see the commands installed into it. Look for (.venv) at the start of the prompt and activate it again if it's missing. python -m fastapi --version also works, because it goes through the active Python directly.

⚠️ `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fastapi'` when you press Run

FastAPI is installed, but VS Code ran a different Python. Open the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P or Cmd+Shift+P), run Python: Select Interpreter, and choose the one inside .venv. Then open a fresh terminal.

#See a virtual environment made from scratch

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You install FastAPI, close VS Code, reopen it, and fastapi dev now says command not found. What's the most likely cause?

  • Packages stay in .venv until you delete the folder.

  • Activation only lasts for one terminal session. Check for (.venv) and activate again.

  • Uvicorn came with fastapi[standard], and a missing server would give a different error.

Show answer

B. Activation only lasts for one terminal session. Check for (.venv) and activate again.

2Why does this course install with python -m pip instead of plain pip?

  • Speed is the same; the difference is where the package goes.

  • Plain pip can belong to a different Python than the one you run, which is the classic "I installed it but Python can't find it" problem.

  • Both can install extras. The quotes matter for zsh; python -m matters for picking the right Python.

Show answer

B. Plain pip can belong to a different Python than the one you run, which is the classic "I installed it but Python can't find it" problem.

3In Windows PowerShell, curl --version prints a red error instead of a version number. What's going on?

  • Windows 10 and 11 include it as curl.exe.

  • Windows PowerShell maps the short name to its own command. Adding .exe runs the real curl.

Show answer

B. Windows PowerShell maps the short name to its own command. Adding .exe runs the real curl.

Key takeaways

  • Uvicorn receives HTTP, FastAPI routes and checks it, and your function produces the answer.
  • Every project gets its own .venv. Activate it in each new terminal and look for (.venv) in the prompt.
  • Install with python -m pip install "fastapi[standard]". The quotes protect the brackets and python -m picks the right Python.
  • On Windows PowerShell, type curl.exe.

#Further reading

  • FastAPI: Virtual Environments (opens in a new tab): FastAPI's own guide, with diagrams of what activation changes and why it matters.
  • Python Environments in VS Code (opens in a new tab): how VS Code finds, creates, and selects environments.
  • venv in the Python docs (opens in a new tab): the activation command for every shell, including the PowerShell execution policy note.

m1-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write a FastAPI app with two routes and start it with fastapi dev main.py.
  • Read the startup output and the one-line log each request leaves behind.
  • Call the same route four ways: browser, curl -i, the /docs page, and TestClient.
  • Fix "address already in use", a wrong file name, and a server that didn't reload.

Here's the finish line for this lesson. You type a URL into a second terminal, and your own code answers:

That is a complete HTTP response: a status line, some headers, a blank line, and a body. You'll take it apart properly in Module 2. For now, the goal is to make one.

#Step 1: Write the app

Inside backend-course, make a folder called hello and a file inside it called main.py:

Three things are going on. app = FastAPI() creates the application object the server will look for. @app.get("/") registers the function below it as the handler for GET requests to the path /. And whatever you return (here a dict) is converted to JSON for you.

The second route has {name} in its path. That's a path parameter: whatever the client puts in that spot arrives as the name argument. Running this file with the play button prints nothing, because it only defines things. A server has to load it.

#Step 2: Start the server

In the VS Code terminal, with (.venv) showing:

FastAPI prints a block like this (trimmed here):

Read it top to bottom. FastAPI found app inside main.py, Uvicorn is listening at 127.0.0.1 (your own computer, also called localhost) on port 8000, and a reloader is watching your files. The terminal is now busy serving, so it won't take new commands until you press Ctrl+C.

#Step 3: Visit it in a browser

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000 (opens in a new tab). The page shows {"message":"Hello from FastAPI"}. Now try http://127.0.0.1:8000/hello/Ada, and then a path that doesn't exist, such as /nope.

Look back at the server terminal. Each visit left a line:

That line is the server's view of the conversation: who asked, the method, the path, and the status code it sent back. /nope got 404 and the body {"detail":"Not Found"}, because no route matches that path. When something goes wrong later in the course, this log is the first place to look.

#Step 4: Ask with curl

The first terminal is running the server, so open a second one with the + button in the terminal panel. curl doesn't need the virtual environment, so it works straight away:

Windows

macOS

Chromebook / Linux

The -i flag means "include the headers". Without it, curl prints only the body. With it, you can see that the server said 200 OK, that it was Uvicorn, and that the body is application/json, 25 bytes long. The browser received the same headers; it just didn't show them.

#Step 5: Change the code while it runs

Edit the greeting to f"Hi there, {name}" and save. Among a few other lines, the server terminal prints:

Run the curl command again and you get the new text. That reload is what the dev in fastapi dev buys you. No save, no reload: if your change isn't showing up, check the file tab in VS Code for the dot that means "unsaved".

#Step 6: Use the /docs page

Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs (opens in a new tab). FastAPI built this page from your code: both routes are listed, with their methods and parameters. Click GET /hello/{name}, then Try it out, type a name, and click Execute.

The page sends a real request to your server and shows the curl command it used, the request URL, the status code, the response body, and the response headers. It's the fastest way to test a route that needs a request body, which you'll do in Module 4. There's a second docs style at /redoc, and the raw description both are built from lives at /openapi.json.

#Step 7: Call the app from Python with TestClient

The last way to talk to your app skips the server entirely. TestClient hands a request straight to the app object and gives you back the response, so it works even when nothing is running. This course uses it for every runnable example and for your tests.

client.get(path) returns a response object with .status_code, .headers, and .json(). Notice %20 in the third path: URLs can't contain spaces, so a space travels as %20, and FastAPI decodes it before your function sees it. In your own project you'd write from main import app instead of copying the routes, which is exactly how the tests in Module 4 start.

#When it doesn't work

⚠️ `[Errno 48] Address already in use` (or `Errno 98`, or `WinError 10048`)

Another server already holds port 8000, usually one you started earlier in another terminal. Find that terminal and press Ctrl+C, or start this one on a different port with fastapi dev main.py --port 8001.

⚠️ `Path does not exist mian.py`

The CLI couldn't find the file you named. Check the spelling, and check that the terminal is in the folder that holds main.py: run cd hello first, or start it from the course folder with fastapi dev hello/main.py.

⚠️ The browser says "This site can't be reached"

Nothing is listening at that address. The server isn't running (look for Application startup complete.), or you typed https:// instead of http://. The development server doesn't do HTTPS.

#Watch someone build the same app

Check your understanding

3 questions

1You change the greeting, refresh the browser, and still see the old text. The server terminal shows no "Reloading" message. What happened?

  • Possible in general, but the missing reload message points at the file, not the browser.

  • WatchFiles reacts to saved files. Save, and the reload message appears.

  • It reloads on every saved change until you stop it.

Show answer

B. WatchFiles reacts to saved files. Save, and the reload message appears.

2You visit http://127.0.0.1:8000/hello with no name. What comes back?

  • The route needs something in the {name} slot; an empty slot doesn't match.

  • /hello and /hello/{name} are different paths, and no route was registered for /hello alone.

  • Nothing crashed. The server just had no route for that path.

Show answer

B. /hello and /hello/{name} are different paths, and no route was registered for /hello alone.

3Your server is stopped. Does client.get("/") from TestClient still work?

  • No network and no Uvicorn are involved, which is why it's handy for tests.

  • That's true for curl and the browser, which go over the network. TestClient doesn't.

Show answer

A. No network and no Uvicorn are involved, which is why it's handy for tests.

Key takeaways

  • @app.get("/path") connects a method and a path to a function, and a returned dict becomes JSON.
  • fastapi dev main.py starts Uvicorn on http://127.0.0.1:8000 and reloads every time you save.
  • The server terminal logs every request with its method, path, and status code.
  • Browser, curl -i, /docs, and TestClient are four ways to send the same request. curl shows headers; TestClient needs no server.

#Further reading

  • FastAPI: First Steps (opens in a new tab): the official walkthrough of this same app, including what /openapi.json contains.
  • FastAPI CLI (opens in a new tab): what fastapi dev and fastapi run each do and when to use which.
  • FastAPI: Testing (opens in a new tab): the TestClient guide you'll lean on from Module 4 onward.

m1-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Lay out backend-course so every module has a home and one shared virtual environment.
  • Work with two terminals: one runs the server, one sends requests.
  • Use the status code to decide where to look, and find the traceback behind a 500.
  • Pause a live request in the VS Code debugger and inspect its variables.
  • Save a requirements.txt that rebuilds your environment on any computer.

Sooner or later, the browser will show you two words and nothing else:

That's not much to go on, and it's on purpose. A server shouldn't tell strangers what broke inside it. The full story went somewhere else: to the terminal running the server. Backend work means getting used to the fact that the client and the server see different halves of every problem, and learning to check both.

#A layout that lasts the whole course

Keep everything for this course in the folder you made in the first lesson, with one shared .venv at the top and a folder per project:

Open the backend-course folder itself in VS Code, not a subfolder, so VS Code keeps finding .venv. To run a server, cd into its folder first (cd notes-api) and then run fastapi dev main.py.

#Two terminals, two jobs

A running server holds onto its terminal. So the course always uses two:

  1. Server terminal: fastapi dev main.py. Leave it running and watch it, because every request and every crash shows up here.
  2. Client terminal: curl commands, python -m unittest, anything else. Open it with the + button in the terminal panel, or select the split icon to see both side by side.

If you lose track of which is which, the server terminal is the one where you can't type.

#How the code on these pages runs

Code blocks with an Output box underneath were run when this page was built. For an API, that means a TestClient sent a real request to a real FastAPI app, and the box shows exactly what came back. Your output can differ in small ways (newer package versions, today's date in a header), but status codes and JSON should match. Blocks without an Output box are files to save or commands to type.

#Let the status code tell you where to look

Every response carries a status code, and the code narrows down where the problem is before you read a single line of your own code.

Here's a small app with a bug in it. Predict what each of the four requests gets before you read the output.

Line by line: ana works. Ana with a capital A isn't a key in the dict, so the function crashed and the client got a bare 500. The POST found the path but no POST route, so it's 405 Method Not Allowed. And /scores by itself matches nothing, so 404.

Now the other half. When curl got that 500, the server terminal printed this (shortened here; the real one runs past 60 lines):

Most of that traceback is FastAPI's and Uvicorn's machinery, so skip to the bottom. The last file that's yours (main.py, line 9) and the last line (KeyError: 'Ana') are the whole story. The fix is to handle the missing key on purpose and send a proper 404 with a reason:

raise HTTPException(...) stops the function and sends that status and message to the client. You'll use it constantly from Module 4 on. A rule worth keeping: a 500 always means the server has a bug, even when the client sent something silly. The server's job is to answer bad input with a 4xx that says what was wrong.

#Pause a request with the debugger

When reading the traceback isn't enough, stop the server mid-request and look around. Stop fastapi dev with Ctrl+C, open main.py, and click in the margin to the left of a line number inside your route to set a breakpoint (a red dot appears). Press F5 and choose the FastAPI option from the list (if VS Code asks for a debugger first, pick Python Debugger).

The server starts under the debugger. Send a request from the browser or curl, and it seems to hang: your code is paused on the breakpoint. The Run and Debug view shows every variable, including name exactly as it arrived. Press F5 again to continue, and the response goes out.

💡 Tip

The debugger runs the app without reload, so stop it (Shift+F5) and go back to fastapi dev main.py once you've found the bug.

#Save your setup, not just your code

.venv is big and specific to your computer, so never copy or share it. Record what's in it instead. The simplest version is a one-line requirements.txt in backend-course:

On a new computer (or after deleting a broken .venv), make a fresh environment, activate it, and run:

⚠️ `pip freeze` from a Mac breaks on Windows

python -m pip freeze > requirements.txt pins the exact version of every installed package, which sounds safer. But FastAPI's standard extras include uvloop on macOS and Linux only, and freeze writes it down without that condition, so the same file fails to install on Windows. For this course, the one-line file is more portable. If you use Git, add .venv/ to your .gitignore.

#Asking for help that gets a useful answer

When you post a question to a classmate, a forum, or a teacher, include four things. With all four, most people can spot the problem in a minute:

  1. The exact request: the full curl command, or the method and URL.
  2. The full response, from curl -i so the status and headers are included.
  3. The route function's code.
  4. The bottom of the server traceback, from the last line that's yours to the end.

#See the debugger in action

Check your understanding

3 questions

1curl prints Internal Server Error and nothing else. Where is the useful information?

  • The headers say it's a 500 and plain text, but not why.

  • The server logs the crash where only you can see it, and the last lines name the file, line, and exception.

  • The URL tells you what was asked, not what went wrong.

Show answer

B. The server logs the crash where only you can see it, and the last lines name the file, line, and exception.

2POST /scores/ana returns 405 Method Not Allowed. What does that tell you?

  • A 405 means "found the path, not that method". The response even includes an Allow: GET header.

  • A crash is a 500. A 405 is the router saying no before your code runs.

  • A misspelled path would give a 404.

Show answer

A. A 405 means "found the path, not that method". The response even includes an Allow: GET header.

3Why does this course suggest a one-line requirements.txt instead of pip freeze?

  • Speed isn't the issue.

  • The one-line file lets pip choose the right packages for each operating system.

  • It includes FastAPI and everything else in the environment, which is the problem.

Show answer

B. The one-line file lets pip choose the right packages for each operating system.

Key takeaways

  • Keep one .venv at the top of backend-course and a folder per project. Open the top folder in VS Code.
  • Run the server in one terminal and send requests from another.
  • Use the status code to decide where to look first. For a 500, read the bottom of the server traceback.
  • A 500 is always the server's bug: catch the problem and send a 4xx with a reason instead.
  • Share requirements.txt, never .venv.

#Further reading

  • Python debugging in VS Code (opens in a new tab): every debugger feature, including conditional breakpoints for "only stop when name is Ana".
  • FastAPI: Handling Errors (opens in a new tab): more on HTTPException, which Module 4 uses for every missing resource.
  • pip User Guide: Requirements Files (opens in a new tab): how -r requirements.txt works and what else you can put in the file.

m2-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Name the parts of an HTTP request (method, URL, headers, body) and of a response (status, headers, body).
  • Split a URL into scheme, host, path, and query string, and encode a query safely.
  • Choose between GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE, and explain which are safe and idempotent.
  • Read a status code's class at a glance and know what 200, 201, 204, 304, 400, 401, 404, 422, and 500 mean.
  • Parse a JSON body and check the status before trusting it.

A weather app on your phone says "Couldn't load data." Three suspects: the phone sent a bad request, the server broke, or the answer came back in a shape the app didn't expect. Picking the right suspect is most of backend debugging, and you can do it because HTTP is plain text. You can read the whole conversation.

Here's a real one. curl -v prints the lines it sends (starting with >) and the lines it receives (starting with <). This asked GitHub's public API about a user named octocat:

The request is four lines. The response is a status line, some headers, a blank line, and a body. Everything in this module is about reading those parts.

#Clients ask, servers answer

HTTP has two roles. The client (a browser, a phone app, curl, your Python script) always speaks first. The server waits, answers each request with exactly one response, and then forgets about it. That forgetting is called being stateless: each request has to carry everything the server needs, because the server keeps no memory of the conversation so far.

#A URL is four parts

https://api.github.com/users/octocat/repos?per_page=2&sort=updated packs a lot into one line. Python's urllib.parse will take it apart for you:

The scheme (https) says how to connect, the host says which computer, and the path says which thing on that computer. The query string after ? holds optional settings as name=value pairs joined with &. Notice that parse_qs gives you lists, since a name can appear more than once, and every value is a string: '2', not 2. In the last line, the space became + and the & inside a value became %26, so it can't be mistaken for a separator.

#Watch a server pull a request apart

What reaches a server is just text. Here's the core of what a server does first with every request, stripped down to plain Python. Step through it and watch headers fill up.

The blank line (\r\n\r\n) is what separates the head from the body, which is empty for this GET. Header names are lowercased because HTTP treats Accept and accept as the same header. That's why GitHub's response above uses all-lowercase names. Uvicorn does all of this for you, with many more checks.

#Methods say what you want done

The first word of the request is the method. It tells the server what kind of action you want on the thing the path names.

Method Means Has a body? Safe? Idempotent?
GET Read it No Yes Yes
POST Create something new under it Yes No No
PUT Replace it completely Yes No Yes
PATCH Change some of its fields Yes No Usually not
DELETE Remove it Usually no No Yes

Safe means the request doesn't change anything on the server, so browsers and tools may send it freely. Idempotent means sending it twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once. Deleting note 3 twice still leaves note 3 deleted, even though the second response is a 404. Posting the same new note twice makes two notes, which is why a payment form warns you not to click "Pay" twice.

#Status codes are the server's one-word answer

The first digit tells you who should act next:

  • 2xx success: 200 OK, 201 Created (something new exists now), 204 No Content (it worked; nothing to send back).
  • 3xx look elsewhere: 301/302 redirects, and 304 Not Modified ("your saved copy is still good").
  • 4xx the client must change something: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (who are you?), 403 Forbidden (I know who you are; still no), 404 Not Found, 422 Unprocessable Content (I understood the request, but the data breaks the rules).
  • 5xx the server failed: 500 Internal Server Error, 503 Service Unavailable.

Python ships with the official list:

GitHub's API shows several of these in practice. Asking for a user who doesn't exist gets 404 with the body {"message": "Not Found", ...}. Trying to create a repository with POST /user/repos without logging in gets 401 and {"message": "Requires authentication", ...}. Same server, same format, different code, and the code alone already tells you whose move it is.

#Headers carry the details

Headers are name: value lines about the message itself. A few you'll see constantly:

  • content-type says what the body is. application/json means "parse me as JSON."
  • content-length is the body's size in bytes (1350 for octocat).
  • accept (from the client) says what formats it can handle. curl's */* means "anything."
  • user-agent names the client program.
  • cache-control and etag let clients reuse a response instead of downloading it again.
  • x-ratelimit-remaining is GitHub's own header: 49 more requests allowed this hour from this address without logging in.

#The body is usually JSON

JSON is text that looks a lot like Python literals, with a few differences: strings always use double quotes, true/false/null are lowercase, and there are no tuples or comments. json.loads turns JSON text into Python objects:

false became False and null became None. Numbers stay numbers, so public_repos + 1 works. Values in a query string are always strings, while a JSON body keeps its types.

⚠️ Python's dict syntax isn't JSON

A dict printed by Python uses single quotes, and pasting it as JSON fails:

The error points at character 1, the first single quote. Use json.dumps(data) to make JSON from Python, never str(data).

⚠️ Unquoted `&` and `?` in the terminal

Type curl https://api.github.com/users/octocat/repos?per_page=2&sort=updated without quotes and zsh answers no matches found, bash quietly drops everything after &, and PowerShell refuses with an error about the ampersand. Wrap every URL that has a query string in double quotes.

⚠️ Check the status before using the body

A 404 still has a JSON body, just a different one. Code that reads data["login"] without checking the status first will crash with a KeyError the first time a user doesn't exist. Check status_code (or the HTTP/2 404 line) first.

#Hear it explained another way

Check your understanding

4 questions

1In https://api.github.com/users/octocat/repos?per_page=2&sort=updated, what is per_page=2&sort=updated?

  • The path is /users/octocat/repos; it ends at the ?.

  • Everything after ? is the query, split into pairs at each &.

  • Headers travel on their own lines, not in the URL.

Show answer

B. Everything after ? is the query, split into pairs at each &.

2A client sends DELETE /notes/3, gets 204, then sends it again and gets 404. Is DELETE still idempotent here?

  • Idempotence is about the effect on the server, not about getting identical responses.

  • The responses differ, but the state of the server after one call and after two calls is the same.

Show answer

A. Idempotence is about the effect on the server, not about getting identical responses.

3What does json.loads('{"done": true, "due": null}') return?

  • JSON keeps its types: true is a boolean, not text.

  • JSON true becomes Python True, and null becomes None.

  • Lowercase is correct in JSON. Python's True would be the error.

Show answer

B. JSON true becomes Python True, and null becomes None.

4An app gets 401 back from an API. Who needs to change something?

  • Server failures are 5xx.

  • 4xx codes ask the client to change the request, and 401 specifically asks for authentication.

  • Only 2xx codes mean success.

Show answer

B. 4xx codes ask the client to change the request, and 401 specifically asks for authentication.

Key takeaways

  • A request is a method, a URL, headers, and an optional body. A response is a status, headers, and a body.
  • The URL's query string holds optional name=value settings, and every value arrives as text.
  • GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH changes part, DELETE removes. GET, PUT, and DELETE are idempotent.
  • 2xx worked, 3xx look elsewhere, 4xx the client must fix something, 5xx the server failed.
  • Check the status first, then parse the JSON body.

#Further reading

  • MDN: An overview of HTTP (opens in a new tab): clear diagrams of clients, servers, and proxies, from the people who document the web platform.
  • MDN: HTTP messages (opens in a new tab): the exact layout of requests and responses, including the blank line.
  • MDN: HTTP response status codes (opens in a new tab): every code with a short description. Worth bookmarking.

What you'll learn

  • Send GET requests with curl and curl -i, and save full responses with -o.
  • Use a query string to ask for one page of results, and find the next page in the link header.
  • Write parse_response(), which splits a saved response into status, headers, and parsed body.
  • Handle an error response without crashing.

You'll ask GitHub's API three questions from the terminal, save each answer to a file, and then write read_response.py, a script that reads all three files and reports what happened. Here's what it prints when it's done:

One line per exchange, with exactly the facts you'd want when debugging: did it work, what came back, is there more, and how many requests you have left. Make a folder called http-practice inside backend-course and work there.

On Windows, type curl.exe wherever these steps say curl.

#Step 1: A request with no surprises

Start with the simplest endpoint GitHub has. It returns one line of plain text:

You'll get a different saying each time, because the server picks one at random. Now add -i to include the response head:

That's trimmed to five of the 22 headers GitHub sent. The content-type is text/plain, so this body isn't JSON. content-length: 35 counts the bytes in the saying, and x-ratelimit-remaining dropped by one, because every request you send without logging in counts against the 60 you're allowed each hour.

#Step 2: Ask for JSON and save it

Now ask about a user, and save the whole response, head and body, to a file:

-s (silent) hides curl's progress meter and -o octocat.txt writes the output to a file instead of the screen. Use -o rather than > octocat.txt: Windows PowerShell saves redirected output as UTF-16, which Python then reads as gibberish, while -o lets curl write the bytes itself.

Open octocat.txt in VS Code. It's the same response you saw in the last lesson: a status line, about 25 headers, a blank line, and a JSON body.

#Step 3: Get the files onto this page

This page can't use the network, so the next cell recreates your three files exactly as curl saved them, trimmed to the headers and fields this build uses. On your computer, skip this cell: you'll have real files from curl. (Run the two curl commands in Steps 5 and 6 now if you want all three files before writing any Python.)

#Step 4: Split a response into its parts

Every response has the same layout, so one function can read them all. The blank line separates the head from the body, the first line of the head is the status line, and every other head line is name: value.

A few decisions in there are worth a second look. partition("\n\n") splits at the first blank line only, so a body that contains blank lines stays in one piece. int(...) turns the status into a number, so later code can write status >= 400. Lowercasing header names means Content-Type and content-type land on the same key. And the body only goes through json.loads when the server said it was JSON.

📝 Note

curl writes the head with \r\n line endings, as HTTP requires. read_text() converts them to \n as it reads, which is why splitting on "\n\n" works on the real files too.

#Step 5: Ask for one page at a time

A user with thousands of repos can't get them all in one response, so GitHub hands them out in pages. You choose the page size with a query string, which means quotes around the URL:

The body is a JSON list of two repos, and the head includes a link header that says where the rest are:

Two links, each labeled with a rel: next is page 2, and last is page 4. Four pages of two is eight repos, matching octocat's public_repos: 8. Pull the labels out with a function:

page_number reuses the URL tools from the last lesson: split the link into parts, parse its query, and take the first page value. A client that wants every repo keeps following next until a response arrives without one.

#Step 6: An answer you didn't want

Ask for a user who doesn't exist:

The body is still JSON, just a different shape: {"message": "Not Found", ...}. Code that expects a user would crash here, so the summary function checks the status first and only then decides how to read the body:

#The finished script

Here's read_response.py in one piece. Save it in http-practice next to your three files and run it with the play button.

🧪 Try it yourself

Save a fourth response with curl -s -i "https://api.github.com/users/octocat/repos?per_page=2&page=4" -o last.txt, add "last.txt" to FILES, and run it again. The last page has no next link, so that part of the line disappears.

#Watch curl used on a different API

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does summarize check status >= 400 before reading data["login"]?

  • GitHub's 404 has a JSON body. It just has message instead of login.

  • The status tells you which shape to expect, so it has to be read first.

  • It reads them fine. The status line has the same layout for every response.

Show answer

B. The status tells you which shape to expect, so it has to be read first.

2Why does the build save responses with curl -o file instead of curl > file?

  • With -o, curl writes the bytes itself on every system, so the file is the same everywhere.

  • The headers come from -i. Redirection would keep them.

  • The request is identical; only where the output goes differs.

Show answer

A. With -o, curl writes the bytes itself on every system, so the file is the same everywhere.

3The last link says page=4 and you asked for per_page=2. What does that tell you?

  • Four is the number of pages, not repos.

  • Pages 1 to 3 hold two each, and page 4 holds the rest. octocat's profile says 8.

Show answer

B. Pages 1 to 3 hold two each, and page 4 holds the rest. octocat's profile says 8.

Key takeaways

  • curl -i shows the head and body. -s -i URL -o file saves both exactly as received.
  • Quote every URL that has a query string.
  • One parser fits every response: status line, name: value headers, blank line, body.
  • Paginated APIs say where the next page is. GitHub puts it in the link header.
  • Check the status before you assume what the body looks like.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add the etag header to each summary line. Then look up the If-None-Match request header in the MDN guide below and work out what a 304 response would mean for your script.
  • Show the rate limit's reset time: x-ratelimit-reset is a Unix timestamp, which datetime.fromtimestamp() converts.
  • Open your browser's developer tools on any website, choose the Network tab, and reload. Every row is a request like the ones you just made, with the same headers.

m2-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Split URLs and build query strings that survive spaces, &, and +.
  • Decide from a status code who has to act next.
  • Diagnose a failed exchange from its request and response alone.
  • Build and parse raw HTTP messages, counting content-length in bytes.

These exercises use only Python's standard library, so you can do them in http-practice without a server running. Try each one before opening the solution. When your output matches the sample, you're done.

#Warm-up: who moves next?

Without looking anything up, say who has to act after each response: the client, the server's developers, or nobody.

201 · 304 · 403 · 422 · 503 · 204

Show solution

201 and 204: nobody, it worked. 304: nobody, really; the client uses the copy it already has. 403 and 422: the client, which must change the request (or accept the answer). 503: the server's side, since it's down or overloaded, and the client can only try again later.

#Exercise 1: Take a URL apart

Write describe(url) that prints the host, the path as a list of segments, and the query as a dict of single values (not lists). Test it on https://api.github.com/repos/fastapi/fastapi/issues?state=open&per_page=5.

Need a hint?

urlsplit gives you .netloc, .path, and .query. Split the path on / and drop empty strings. parse_qs returns lists, so keep the first item of each.

Show solution

The path starts with /, so splitting it gives an empty string first; the if piece filter drops it. Notice '5' is still a string. Query values are always text until your code converts them.

#Exercise 2: Build a search URL safely

Write search_url(text, page=1) that returns a GitHub repository search URL like https://api.github.com/search/repositories?q=...&page=.... It must work for "fastapi tutorial" and for "c++ & rust".

Need a hint?

Gluing strings with f-strings breaks on the second example: the & would start a new parameter, and the server would read each + as a space. urllib.parse.urlencode takes a dict and escapes every value.

Show solution

+ became %2B because in a query string a bare + means a space. Without the encoding, the pluses would turn into spaces, the server would search for just c, and rust would arrive as a stray parameter with no value.

#Exercise 3: Who acts next, in code

Write who_acts(code) that returns "nobody" for 2xx, "client (redirect or cache)" for 3xx, "client (fix the request)" for 4xx, and "server" for 5xx. Anything outside 100–599 should raise ValueError. Then print a line for [200, 304, 404, 422, 500, 99].

Need a hint?

Integer division by 100 gives the class: 404 // 100 is 4. Handle the 1xx informational codes however you like; the sample doesn't use one.

Show solution

A lookup dict keyed by the first digit replaces a chain of if statements, and the range check runs first so 99 // 100 (which is 0) never reaches the lookup.

#Exercise 4: Diagnose four failed exchanges

For each one, say which side is at fault and what change fixes it. No code needed.

  1. In bash, curl https://api.github.com/users/octocat/repos?per_page=2&sort=updated returns two repos, but not sorted by update time.
  2. POST /notes with body {"text": "Buy milk"} returns 422 and {"detail":[{"type":"missing","loc":["body","title"],"msg":"Field required"}]}.
  3. GET /notes/7 returns 500 and the plain text Internal Server Error.
  4. DELETE /notes returns 405 and the header allow: GET, POST.
Need a hint?

For each, read the status class first, then the detail. loc in a 422 is a path to the bad field. An allow header lists the methods the path does accept.

Show solution
# At fault Fix
1 Client (the shell) The unquoted & sent curl to the background with only per_page=2. Quote the URL.
2 Client The server wants title, and loc: ["body", "title"] says so. Send {"title": "Buy milk"}.
3 Server A 500 is always a server bug. Read the traceback in the server terminal and handle that case with a 4xx.
4 Client /notes is the whole collection and doesn't accept DELETE. Delete one note: DELETE /notes/7.

#Exercise 5: Build a response by hand

Write make_response(status, data) that returns the full bytes of an HTTP/1.1 response: status line, content-type: application/json, a correct content-length, a blank line, and the JSON body. Lines end in \r\n. Test it with {"city": "São Paulo"}, keeping the ã as is.

Need a hint?

content-length counts bytes, not characters. ã is one character but two bytes in UTF-8, so len() of the string gives the wrong answer. Encode first, then measure.

Show solution

The string is 21 characters but 22 bytes. A server that sent content-length: 21 would cut off the closing }, and the client's JSON parser would fail on a response that looks fine when you print it.

#Exercise 6: Parse a request with a body

A server receives this text. Write parse_request(raw) that returns a dict with method, path, query (single values), headers (lowercase names), and json (the parsed body, or None if the content type isn't JSON).

Need a hint?

Reuse the trace from the Notes lesson for the head, partition("?") for the query, and only call json.loads when the content type contains json. (The Content-Length here is wrong on purpose; the solution explains why that matters.)

Show solution

partition(":") splits at the first colon only, which matters for the Host header: its value 127.0.0.1:8000 contains another colon. The last line shows the body is 42 bytes, not 39. A real server trusts Content-Length to know where the body ends, so it would read 39 bytes and hand your code broken JSON. Libraries like curl and httpx compute it for you, which is a good reason never to set it by hand.

#Challenge: Answer "has it changed?" with an ETag

GitHub sent etag: W/"937b..." with octocat's profile. A client can send that value back in an If-None-Match header, and if nothing changed, the server answers 304 Not Modified with no body. That saves sending 1,350 bytes again.

Write respond(request_headers, data) that computes an ETag from the JSON body (use hashlib.sha256, first 12 hex characters, wrapped in double quotes) and returns (status, headers, body): a 304 with an empty body if If-None-Match matches, otherwise a 200 with the body and an etag header. Show three calls: a first visit, a repeat visit with the ETag, and a visit after the data changed.

Need a hint?

Compute the body bytes first, hash them, then compare with request_headers.get("if-none-match"). Return the etag header on the 304 too, so the client keeps the current value.

Show solution

The hash changes whenever a single byte of the body changes, so the third request gets a full 200 with a new ETag. That's the whole idea behind 304: the client proves which version it has, and the server only sends data when there's something new. GitHub's W/ prefix marks a "weak" ETag, which promises the same meaning rather than identical bytes.

#When you're stuck on status codes

m3-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Name endpoints after resources (nouns) and let the HTTP method be the verb.
  • Choose the right status code for success and for each kind of failure.
  • Write a JSON contract: field names, types, and what null and missing mean.
  • Use one error shape across every endpoint.
  • Explain limit/offset pagination and which changes force a new API version.

A student team built a task app over a weekend. The phone app and the website both talk to its API, and both keep breaking. Here's what the API looks like from the outside:

Each route works, more or less. But a client has to memorize four naming styles, two spellings of title, a boolean spelled "no", two different wrappers, an error that claims success, and one response that isn't JSON at all. Every one of those quirks has to be special-cased in every client, forever.

An API's contract is the set of promises it makes: these URLs, these methods, these status codes, these JSON shapes. REST is a widely used style for writing that contract so that clients can guess correctly. By the end of this lesson, the same API looks like this:

#Name things, and let the method be the verb

The core move of REST is to treat your data as resources with addresses. Tasks are a resource. /tasks is the collection of all tasks and /tasks/7 is one item. The HTTP method then says what to do with it, so the path never needs a verb:

Instead of Write Why
GET /getTasks GET /tasks GET already means "get".
POST /task_create POST /tasks POST to a collection means "add one".
GET /task?id=99 GET /tasks/99 An item's id belongs in the path.
POST /deleteTask?id=3 DELETE /tasks/3 DELETE is idempotent; a POST would look unsafe to retry.
GET /tasks/byProject/7 GET /projects/7/tasks Tasks that belong to project 7 live under it.

A few conventions go with it: plural nouns for collections, lowercase paths with hyphens between words (/study-groups), and the query string for optional things like filters and sorting (/tasks?done=false&sort=due). The path says which resource; the query says how you want it.

A few actions don't fit, like "email a reminder now." Model them as a small resource you create, such as POST /tasks/7/reminders, and use that trick sparingly.

#Choose status codes on purpose

The status code is the one part of a response every client reads, so it must be right. This chart covers most decisions you'll make:

The rule the task app broke: never send 200 with an error inside. Monitoring tools, browsers, fetch(), and every HTTP library treat 2xx as success. A 200 {"error": "no such task"} gets cached, counted as a success, and passed on to code that expects a task.

409 Conflict means the data is fine on its own but clashes with what's stored, like a username that's taken. 422 means the data itself breaks a rule, like an empty title.

#A JSON contract is a promise about shapes

The contract for a task is short:

Field Type Rule
id integer Set by the server. Never changes.
title string 1 to 100 characters.
done boolean true or false, never "no".
due string or null A date like "2026-11-20", or null for no due date.

Every endpoint that returns a task returns this shape. Names use one case (this course uses snake_case), dates use ISO 8601 (YYYY-MM-DD) so they sort correctly as text, and null means only "this field exists and has no value."

A contract is only real if something checks it. Here's a tiny checker run against the old API's response and a correct one:

The old response fails four ways from one object. In Module 4 you'll get this checking for free: a Pydantic model is a contract written in Python, and FastAPI enforces it on every request and response.

#One error shape, everywhere

Clients need to show errors to people, and they can only do that if errors always look the same. This course uses FastAPI's default shape, because your server will produce it automatically:

When the problem is invalid data, detail is a list naming each bad field, with loc giving its location (trimmed here to the three most useful keys):

There's also a standard, RFC 9457 "Problem Details", with fields like type, title, and detail. Either choice is fine. Mixing them is not: a client written for {"detail": ...} shows "undefined" when one endpoint answers {"error": ...}.

#Big lists come in pages

GET /tasks might match 50,000 rows. Sending them all is slow for the server, slow over the network, and useless to a person looking at a screen of ten. So list endpoints return pages, controlled by two query parameters: limit (how many) and offset (how many to skip). The server should also cap limit, say at 100, so nobody can ask for a million.

Some APIs return a bare list and put the next page's URL in a header, as GitHub does. Others wrap it in an envelope like {"items": [...], "total": 57, "limit": 20, "offset": 40}. Either way, the client loops until it runs out. Step through one that collects seven tasks, three per page:

Watch offset go 0, 3, 6; the loop stops when a page comes back short. With exactly six tasks, the client would make one extra request that returns [], which is harmless.

#Plan for change: what breaks clients

You can't update a phone app on thousands of devices whenever you like, so some API changes are safe and some break every old client:

Change Safe?
Add a new endpoint Safe
Add a new field to a response Safe, if clients ignore fields they don't know
Add an optional request field with a default Safe
Rename or remove a response field Breaks clients reading it
Change a field's type ("8" to 8) Breaks
Make an optional request field required Breaks clients that don't send it

Breaking changes go into a new version while the old one keeps running for a while. The simplest scheme puts it in the path, /v1/tasks and /v2/tasks. GitHub uses a header instead: remember x-github-api-version-selected: 2022-11-28 in the octocat response? That told you which version of the contract answered.

⚠️ Verbs in paths multiply forever

/getTasks, /getTask, /getTasksForProject, /getDoneTasks: every new question becomes a new endpoint. With resources, they're all GET /tasks or GET /tasks/7 plus a query string like ?project=7&done=true.

⚠️ Renaming a field "to be consistent"

Changing Title to title is the right fix for the task app, and it's also a breaking change. Ship it as /v2, or return both fields for a while and tell clients when the old one goes away.

#Hear it from another angle

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A user marks task 7 as done. Which request fits REST best?

  • A verb in the path, and POST suggests creating something.

  • Task 7 is the resource, PATCH changes part of it, and the body says which part.

  • GET must not change anything. Browsers and caches may send GETs on their own.

Show answer

B. Task 7 is the resource, PATCH changes part of it, and the body says which part.

2POST /tasks creates task 8 and returns it. What status should it send?

  • It worked, but 200 hides the most useful fact: something new now exists.

  • 201 says a new resource was made, and the body holds it.

  • 204 means there's no body, but this response returns the new task.

Show answer

B. 201 says a new resource was made, and the body holds it.

3GET /tasks/99 and task 99 doesn't exist. Which response is right?

  • Every tool will count this as a success. That's the task app's bug.

  • The status tells machines what happened, and detail in the usual shape tells people.

  • Nothing crashed. The client asked for something that isn't there.

Show answer

B. The status tells machines what happened, and detail in the usual shape tells people.

4You change due from "2026-11-20" to a number of days, like 5. Is that safe for existing clients?

  • Same name, different meaning and type. That needs a new version.

  • Clients depend on the type and meaning too, not just the name.

Show answer

A. Same name, different meaning and type. That needs a new version.

Key takeaways

  • Paths name resources (/tasks, /tasks/7). Methods are the verbs. Queries hold options.
  • 201 for created, 204 for no body, 4xx when the client must change something, 5xx only for server failures. Never 200 with an error inside.
  • A JSON contract fixes names, types, and the meaning of null, and the same shape appears everywhere.
  • Use one error shape. This course uses {"detail": ...}.
  • Page long lists with limit and offset, cap the limit, and version any change that breaks old clients.

#Further reading

  • Microsoft REST API Guidelines (opens in a new tab): the rules Microsoft's own teams follow, with reasoning for each.
  • RFC 9457: Problem Details for HTTP APIs (opens in a new tab): the standard error format, short and readable for an RFC.
  • Stripe API: Errors (opens in a new tab): a widely admired API's error contract, with every field explained.

m3-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write a contract for a notes API: fields, endpoints, status codes, and error shapes.
  • Decide limits and defaults (title length, page size) and write them down.
  • Build a mock in plain Python that follows the contract.
  • Turn example requests and responses into checks that any implementation must pass.

In Module 4 you'll build a notes API in FastAPI, and in later modules you'll give it a database, logins, and a web page. All of that goes faster if the contract is settled first, because the front end and the back end can be built against it at the same time. Today you write that contract, and you make it executable: a list of example exchanges, plus a fake server (a mock) that passes them.

Here's the finished check running against the mock. Next module, the same fifteen examples run against your FastAPI server:

Work in http-practice/notes_contract.py. Every cell on this page shares one Python session, so each step builds on the last.

#Step 1: Define the resource

A note has three fields. Two of them come from the client, and one is the server's job:

Field Type Rule
id integer Set by the server, starting at 1. Never changes, never reused.
title string Required. 1 to 100 characters.
body string Optional, defaults to "". At most 2,000 characters.

"Never reused" is a real decision. If note 1 is deleted and the next note also gets id 1, a client holding a link to /notes/1 would silently open someone else's note. Limits are decisions too: a title with no maximum lets one request store a 50 MB "title".

The validation rules become a function. Problems use the same loc shape FastAPI uses, so clients can find the bad field the same way in the mock and in the real server:

An empty list means the data passes. partial=True is for updates, where the client may send only the fields it wants to change. A missing title is fine there, but a title that is sent still has to follow the rules.

#Step 2: Write the endpoint table

This table is the contract. Put it in a docstring at the top of your file so it travels with the code:

Method and path Request body Success Errors
GET /notes?q=&limit=&offset= none 200, a list of notes 422 bad limit or offset
POST /notes {"title", "body"?} 201, the new note 422 bad fields
GET /notes/{id} none 200, the note 404, 422 id isn't a number
PATCH /notes/{id} any of title, body 200, the updated note 404, 422
DELETE /notes/{id} none 204, no body 404

Errors use {"detail": "..."}, and validation errors use {"detail": [{"loc": [...], "msg": "..."}]}. For the list: q matches title or body, ignoring case; limit is 1 to 100 and defaults to 20; offset defaults to 0.

Three choices here are worth defending. PATCH instead of PUT: a phone app editing a body shouldn't have to resend the title. A bare list from GET /notes: simpler for clients, and nothing needs a total count yet. (Switching to an envelope later would break clients, so it would go in /v2.) No delete-everything endpoint: DELETE /notes would be one typo away from disaster, so it doesn't exist, and asking gets a 405.

#Step 3: The collection functions

Each endpoint becomes a function that returns (status, json). These two handle /notes. Remember from Module 2 that query values arrive as strings, so limit has to be checked and converted:

create_note builds the stored note itself, field by field, instead of saving whatever the client sent. A client that sends {"title": "Hi", "id": 999, "admin": true} gets id 1 and nothing else. That habit matters a lot in Module 6.

#Step 4: The item functions

These handle /notes/{id}. All three start with the same lookup, and all three give the same 404 when it fails:

The 404 check comes before validation in update_note. If you PATCH a note that doesn't exist with bad data, "not found" is the more useful answer; there's no point fixing the data for a note that isn't there.

#Step 5: The router

A real server receives a method and a URL, not a function call. The router's job is to pick the function, and it's the part FastAPI will do for you next module:

Notice the order of questions: does the path exist (404), does it allow this method (405), is the id well formed (422), does the note exist (404 from the function). That order matches what FastAPI does, which is why the mock and the real server will agree.

#Step 6: Examples that check any implementation

Now the most valuable part. Each example is one exchange from the contract: method, URL, body, expected status, and expected JSON. For 422 it's the loc that must appear, not the exact message, because message wording is allowed to change but the field it points at isn't.

check_examples takes a send function instead of calling handle directly. That one choice is what lets you reuse it: in Module 4 you'll write a three-line send that uses TestClient, and the same examples will check your FastAPI server. The last example proves the "never reuse ids" rule: after note 1 is deleted, the next note is 3.

#The finished file

Here's notes_contract.py in one piece, with the endpoint table in a docstring at the top. Run it with the play button. If a change to the mock ever makes an example fail, you've either found a bug or changed the contract, and both are worth knowing before a client finds out.

🧪 Try it yourself

Add an example of your own: ("PATCH", "/notes/2", {"title": "x" * 101}, 422, ["body", "title"]). Predict whether it passes, then run it.

#Watch: what separates good APIs from bad

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the contract say ids are never reused after a delete?

  • It's easy; the risk is what clients do with old ids.

  • Ids are addresses. Reusing one quietly redirects every saved link to the wrong thing.

  • Speed doesn't change. It's about every saved link pointing at the right note.

Show answer

B. Ids are addresses. Reusing one quietly redirects every saved link to the wrong thing.

What you'll learn

  • Turn action-style routes into resources and methods.
  • Pick status codes for cases that look alike: 400 vs 422, 401 vs 403, 404 vs 409.
  • Write code that converts mixed error shapes into one, and pages a list with an envelope.
  • Detect breaking changes between two versions of a response.
  • Explain why offset pagination can show the same item twice.

The school library has an API that grew one route at a time. These exercises redesign it piece by piece. The first two are design problems you answer in writing; the rest are code you can run in http-practice.

#Warm-up

Rewrite each route in REST style: GET /fetchAllBooks, POST /addNewMember, GET /bookInfo?isbn=9780441013593.

Show solution

GET /books, POST /members, and GET /books/9780441013593. The id goes in the path, and an ISBN is a fine id for a book because it never changes.

#Exercise 1: Redesign the library's routes

Rewrite all six. Think about which resource each one acts on, and whether something belongs to something else.

  1. POST /checkoutBook?book=12&member=5
  2. GET /getLoansForMember?member=5
  3. POST /returnBook?loan=88
  4. GET /searchBooks?text=dune
  5. POST /updateMemberEmail?member=5&email=ana@school.org
  6. GET /overdueLoans
Need a hint?

A checkout creates something: a loan. Returning a book changes that loan. Searching and "overdue" are filters on a collection, so they belong in the query string.

Show solution
Old New
POST /checkoutBook?book=12&member=5 POST /loans with {"book_id": 12, "member_id": 5}
GET /getLoansForMember?member=5 GET /members/5/loans
POST /returnBook?loan=88 PATCH /loans/88 with {"returned_on": "2026-11-16"}
GET /searchBooks?text=dune GET /books?q=dune
POST /updateMemberEmail?... PATCH /members/5 with {"email": "ana@school.org"}
GET /overdueLoans GET /loans?overdue=true

Turning "checkout" into "create a loan" is the key move: a loan has its own id, dates, and history, so it's a resource in its own right. Notice the data moved from the query string into JSON bodies. An email address in a URL ends up in server logs and browser history.

#Exercise 2: Pick the status code

  1. POST /loans for a book that's already checked out.
  2. POST /loans with {"book_id": "twelve"}.
  3. POST /loans with a body that isn't valid JSON at all: {"book_id": 12.
  4. DELETE /members/5 with no login.
  5. DELETE /members/5, logged in as a student who isn't a librarian.
  6. GET /books/0000000000 for an ISBN that isn't in the catalog.
  7. PATCH /loans/88 that works and returns the updated loan.
  8. DELETE /loans/88 that works.
Need a hint?

Ask, in order: did it work? If not, is the data unreadable, readable but against the rules, or fine but clashing with what's stored? For logins: is it "who are you?" or "I know who you are, and no"?

Show solution
# Code Why
1 409 Conflict The request is valid; it clashes with the book's current state.
2 422 Readable JSON, but book_id breaks the "integer" rule.
3 400 Bad Request The server can't even parse it. (FastAPI actually answers this with 422 too, and a json_invalid error type.)
4 401 Unauthorized No login, so the server doesn't know who's asking.
5 403 Forbidden The server knows who's asking, and they aren't allowed.
6 404 Not Found No such book.
7 200 OK It worked, with a body.
8 204 No Content It worked, with nothing to send back.

#Exercise 3: One error shape

The old API answers errors in three different ways. Write to_detail(body) that converts each into {"detail": "..."} and leaves already-correct errors alone.

Need a hint?

Check the most specific case first: a dict that already has detail. Then each old key. A plain string falls through to the end.

Show solution

The code: 403 inside the second body is dropped on purpose. The status code belongs in the status line, where every tool looks for it, not repeated in the body. A function like this is useful during a migration: put it in front of the old API so clients can switch to one error shape before the server code is rewritten.

#Exercise 4: Pages with an envelope

Write page(items, limit=20, offset=0) that returns {"items", "total", "limit", "offset", "next_offset"}, where next_offset is None on the last page. Raise ValueError if limit is outside 1–100 or offset is negative. Then loop through seven book titles three at a time.

Need a hint?

Slicing never fails: items[6:9] on seven items returns one. The next page starts where this one ended, offset + len(chunk), and there's no next page when that reaches len(items).

Show solution

With next_offset, the client loop is one line of logic: keep going while it isn't None. Unlike the bare-list loop in the Notes lesson, this one never makes an extra request for an empty page. In a FastAPI route, those ValueErrors become 422 responses, which Query(ge=1, le=100) will do for you in Module 4.

#Exercise 5: Spot the breaking changes

Write breaking_changes(old, new) that compares an old example response with a new one and lists every removed field and every type change, looking inside nested objects too. Added fields are safe and shouldn't be reported.

The second line is for v1 compared with itself plus a new tags field.

Need a hint?

Loop over the old keys: anything missing from new was removed. Compare type() of each pair. When both values are dicts, call the function again with a prefix like "owner.".

Show solution

Renaming title to name shows up only as "removed title", because from an old client's point of view that's exactly what happened. owner.id turning into a string is the sneaky one: it looks the same when printed, and it breaks any client that does arithmetic or comparisons with it. Big API teams run checks like this on every change.

#Exercise 6: Design a new resource

Students can form study groups, and each group has members. Write the endpoint table (method, path, success code, error codes) for: listing groups, creating one, viewing one, renaming one, deleting one, listing a group's members, adding a member, and removing a member. Then write one example request and response for adding a member.

Need a hint?

Members of a group are a nested collection: /study-groups/{id}/members. Removing a member deletes the membership, not the student. What should happen if the student is already in the group?

Show solution
Method and path Success Errors
GET /study-groups 200 list 422 bad paging
POST /study-groups 201 group 422
GET /study-groups/{id} 200 group 404
PATCH /study-groups/{id} 200 group 404, 422
DELETE /study-groups/{id} 204 404
GET /study-groups/{id}/members 200 list 404 no such group
POST /study-groups/{id}/members 201 membership 404, 409 already a member, 422
DELETE /study-groups/{id}/members/{student_id} 204 404

Example: POST /study-groups/4/members with {"student_id": 31} returns 201 and {"group_id": 4, "student_id": 31, "joined_on": "2026-11-16"}. Sending it again returns 409 and {"detail": "Student 31 is already in group 4"}. You could argue for making the repeat a harmless 200 instead; either is defensible as long as the contract says which.

#Challenge: Why the feed showed a post twice

A social feed lists posts newest first, three per page, using offset. A user loads page 1, someone publishes a new post, and then the user loads page 2. Show what goes wrong, then fix it with cursor pagination: instead of "skip 3", the client asks for "the 3 posts after the last one I saw" (?after=8).

Write offset_page(items, limit, offset) and cursor_page(items, limit, after=None), run both through that sequence of events, and print the ids each client sees.

Need a hint?

For the cursor version, find the position of the item whose id is after, then slice from the position after it. The new post lands at index 0, which shifts every offset by one but doesn't move any post relative to post 8.

Show solution

With offsets, post 8 appears on both pages: the new post pushed everything down one slot, so "skip 3" now lands on 8 again. (Deleting a post does the opposite and silently skips one.) The cursor says "after post 8", which stays true no matter what's added in front. That's why large feeds, Stripe's API, and GitHub's newer endpoints use cursors. Offsets are still fine for small lists that rarely change, like your notes.

m4-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Register routes with @app.get, @app.post, @app.patch, and @app.delete.
  • Read path parameters and query parameters, and let type hints convert and check them.
  • Accept a JSON request body with a Pydantic model and read FastAPI's 422 errors.
  • Control what goes out with a response model and status_code.
  • Send a 404 with HTTPException, and avoid the route-order trap.

In the last module, your mock needed six lines to reject /notes/abc. Here's the FastAPI version. The only check is a type hint:

note_id: int did two jobs. For /notes/7, FastAPI converted the text "7" from the URL into the integer 7 before calling your function. For /notes/abc, it never called your function at all: it answered 422 with loc: ["path", "note_id"], the same shape your contract promised. That's the idea behind FastAPI: you describe what the input should look like with types, and it does the checking.

Every cell on this page shares one Python session, so later cells reuse client and the imports.

#What happens between the request and your function

A route is three things: a method, a path, and a function. @app.get("/notes/{note_id}") adds one to the app's list. You can look at that list yourself:

When a request arrives, FastAPI walks that list in order and uses the first route whose method and path match. If the path matches but no method does, that's a 405; if no path matches, a 404.

#Path parameters, and the route-order trap

A path parameter is a {name} slot in the path that becomes a function argument of the same name. Its type hint decides how it's converted. Without a hint, it stays a string.

The first-match rule causes a classic bug. Suppose you add a "latest note" route after the item route:

/notes/latest matched /notes/{note_id} first, with note_id = "latest", and that failed the int check. The latest_note function never ran. Step through a stripped-down router to see the first-match rule happen:

The fix is to declare fixed paths before paths with parameters: put /notes/latest above /notes/{note_id} in the file.

#Query parameters: every other argument

Any function argument that isn't in the path and isn't a Pydantic model is read from the query string. Give it a default and it's optional; leave the default off and it's required. Extra rules, like a range, go in Query(...), wrapped in Annotated:

ge=1, le=100 means "greater than or equal to 1, less than or equal to 100". Compare this with read_int in your mock: the conversion from text, the range check, and the 422 with a precise message all came from one line of type information. The defaults also show up on the /docs page, so clients can see them.

#Request bodies: a Pydantic model

For POST, PUT, and PATCH, the data travels as JSON in the body. Describe its shape with a Pydantic model, a class that lists fields with types and rules, and use it as a parameter type. FastAPI reads the body, parses the JSON, and validates it against the model:

Read the output slowly. The first request reached your function (the function got: line) as a real NoteIn object with body filled in from its default. The next two never reached it: 422, with loc naming the field and msg saying what's wrong. The last one shows that unknown fields like admin are dropped silently; Module 6 shows how to reject them instead.

status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED sets the success code. status.HTTP_201_CREATED is just the number 201 with a readable name, and without it every route answers 200. note.model_dump() turns the model back into a plain dict.

#Response models: control what goes out

The return type tells FastAPI what the response must look like. It validates your return value against it and drops any fields the model doesn't list. That protects you from leaking something by accident:

The stored record has an owner_email, the function returned all of it, and the client got only the three fields Note declares. You can write response_model=Note in the decorator instead of -> Note; they do the same thing. A return type of -> list[Note] describes a list of them.

#Sending errors with HTTPException

For a missing note, raise HTTPException with a status and a detail. FastAPI stops the function and sends {"detail": ...}:

raise, not return. Returning an HTTPException would try to send the exception object itself as a response.

⚠️ A missing type hint makes every lookup fail

Write def get_note(note_id): without : int, and note_id arrives as the string "1". The dict's keys are integers, so "1" not in NOTES is true and every note returns 404, including ones that exist. The fix is the type hint, which converts the text before your code runs.

⚠️ curl `-d` without a Content-Type header

curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/notes -d '{"title": "Hi"}' sends the body labeled as form data, not JSON. FastAPI answers 422 with loc: ["body"] and "Input should be a valid dictionary or object". Add -H "Content-Type: application/json". TestClient's json= sets that header for you.

#Watch the same ideas in a bigger app

Check your understanding

4 questions

1With def get_note(note_id: int), what does GET /notes/007 return?

  • FastAPI converts "007" to the integer 7 before calling your function.

  • That's what you'd get with no type hint. The hint makes it an integer.

  • "007" is a valid integer, so it passes. "abc" or "1.5" would fail.

Show answer

A. FastAPI converts "007" to the integer 7 before calling your function.

2/notes/{note_id} is declared above /notes/latest. A client requests /notes/latest. What happens?

  • FastAPI doesn't prefer exact matches. It uses the first route in the list that fits.

  • First match wins. Declare /notes/latest first to fix it.

  • Exactly one route handles each request.

Show answer

B. First match wins. Declare /notes/latest first to fix it.

3A route returns {"id": 1, "title": "Hi", "body": "", "password": "x"} and its return type is -> Note (fields id, title, body). What does the client get?

  • The response model filters the output.

  • Fields the response model doesn't declare are dropped before the JSON is sent.

  • Extra fields in the return value are dropped, not treated as errors.

Show answer

B. Fields the response model doesn't declare are dropped before the JSON is sent.

4Your POST /notes route works, but clients see 200 instead of 201. What's missing?

  • That would send the number 201 as the body.

  • The default success code is 200. The decorator sets a different one.

Show answer

B. The default success code is 200. The decorator sets a different one.

Key takeaways

  • A route is a method, a path, and a function. FastAPI uses the first route that matches, so declare fixed paths before {param} paths.
  • Path and query parameters are converted and checked by their type hints. Annotated[int, Query(ge=1, le=100)] adds a range.
  • A Pydantic model as a parameter means "read this from the JSON body". Bad data gets a 422 before your function runs.
  • The return type (or response_model) filters and checks what goes out. status_code= sets the success code.
  • raise HTTPException(404, "...") sends {"detail": "..."}.

#Further reading

  • FastAPI: Path Parameters (opens in a new tab): type conversion, the order trap, and predefined values with enums.
  • FastAPI: Request Body (opens in a new tab): how FastAPI decides whether a parameter comes from the path, the query, or the body.
  • FastAPI: Response Model (opens in a new tab): filtering output, and separate input and output models.
