What you'll learn

  • Write input, update, and output models for a note with Pydantic.
  • Implement create, list, read, update, and delete routes that follow the Module 3 contract.
  • Share one lookup helper so every route gives the same 404.
  • Send real requests with curl and the /docs page.
  • Write unittest tests with TestClient that start from a clean store every time.

This is the notes API from your contract, built for real. When you're done, this is what creating a note from the terminal looks like:

And six tests, run in under a second, check the parts most likely to break. Make a folder called notes-api inside backend-course. Everything in this build goes in notes-api/main.py, except the tests, which go in notes-api/test_main.py. Every cell on this page shares one Python session, so each step adds to the app from the step before.

#Step 1: Models and storage

The contract has three shapes, so the code has three models. NoteIn is what a client sends to create a note. NoteUpdate is what it sends to change one: every field is optional. Note is what the API sends back, and it's the only one with an id, because the server assigns ids.

notes is a plain list, so every note disappears when the server stops. That's fine for now; Module 5 replaces it with a database. ids = count(1) is a counter from itertools: each next(ids) hands out the next number, and nothing ever hands one back, which is exactly the "never reuse ids" rule.

find_note raises instead of returning None. Every route that needs a note calls it, so a missing note gives the same 404 with the same message everywhere, and no route can forget the check.

#Step 2: Create and list

Note(id=next(ids), **note_in.model_dump()) builds the stored note from validated fields plus a server-made id, the same habit as the mock. [offset : offset + limit] does the paging, and the Query rules handle the 422 for limit=0 without a line of your own code.

#Step 3: Read one note

One line of function body, three behaviors: 200 from the helper, 404 raised by the helper, and 422 from the int hint before the function runs.

#Step 4: Update part of a note

PATCH should change only what the client sends. Fields the client leaves out arrive in NoteUpdate as None, so model_dump(exclude_none=True) gives just the fields that were sent:

The first line shows the trick: only body survives. setattr(note, field, value) then changes that one attribute on the stored note. Since notes holds that same object, the change is saved. An empty title still gets a 422, because NoteUpdate keeps the same rules for any field that is sent.

📝 Note

With this design, {"title": null} is treated as "leave the title alone." That's a reasonable rule for this API, since a note can't have no title. An API where null means "clear this field" would use exclude_unset=True instead, which keeps fields the client sent even when they're null.

#Step 5: Delete

204 means "done, no body", so the function returns nothing and the response text is empty. The second delete gets a 404 from the helper. DELETE is still idempotent: note 1 is gone either way.

#Step 6: Run it for real

Put Steps 1 to 5 together in notes-api/main.py (the full file is below), leaving out the client and print lines, which are only for this page. Then, in your server terminal:

Now send requests from your second terminal. A JSON body is easiest to send from a file, because then the quoting is the same on every system. Save {"title": "Buy milk", "body": "2 cartons"} as notes-api/note.json, then:

Windows

macOS

Chromebook / Linux

-X POST sets the method, -H adds a header, and --data "@note.json" sends the file's contents as the body. The first command prints the 201 Created response at the top of this page. The list prints [{"id":1,"title":"Buy milk","body":"2 cartons"}], and note 2 doesn't exist yet:

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs. All five routes are there, with the request body shape for POST and PATCH filled in as an example. Use Try it out to send a PATCH, and watch each request appear in the server terminal with its status code.

⚠️ Forgetting `-H "Content-Type: application/json"`

Without that header, curl labels the body as form data, and FastAPI answers 422 with loc: ["body"] and "Input should be a valid dictionary or object to extract fields from". The JSON was fine; the label was wrong.

#Step 7: Tests that start clean

Clicking around proves it works today. Tests prove it still works after your next round of changes. Each test sends requests with TestClient and checks the answers with assertEqual.

The important part is setUp, which unittest runs before every test. It empties the list, so no test depends on notes another test left behind. The ids keep counting up across tests, which is why the tests use the id that came back from create instead of assuming it's 1.

On your computer, test_main.py starts with from main import app, notes. This page already has both from the cells above, so the cell leaves that line out.

Tests don't need the server, so it doesn't matter whether it's running. From the client terminal, inside notes-api, run python -m unittest -v. unittest finds test_main.py by its name and runs every method that starts with test.

#The finished main.py

About 70 lines for five endpoints, validation, paging, search, consistent errors, and interactive docs. Stop the server and start it again, then list the notes: the list is empty. Keeping notes across restarts is the job of the next module.

#Watch: request and response models in another app

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does NoteUpdate make every field optional, while NoteIn requires title?

  • Required fields on an update model would force clients to resend everything, which is what PUT is for.

  • It does. The difference is a design choice about what each request must contain.

  • Fields that are sent are still validated: an empty title still gets a 422.

Show answer

A. Required fields on an update model would force clients to resend everything, which is what PUT is for.

2Why does find_note raise an HTTPException instead of returning None?

  • It wouldn't crash at that line; the routes would just have to check for it.

  • One helper, one rule. A route can't forget the check because the helper does it.

  • You could also raise the exception inside each route. The helper avoids repeating it.

Show answer

B. One helper, one rule. A route can't forget the check because the helper does it.

3Why does setUp call notes.clear()?

  • Speed is the same. It's about each test starting from a known state.

  • Without it, the filter test would also find notes created by other tests, and results would depend on the order tests run in.

Show answer

B. Without it, the filter test would also find notes created by other tests, and results would depend on the order tests run in.

Key takeaways

  • Use separate models for input (NoteIn), partial updates (NoteUpdate), and output (Note). Only the server sets id.
  • One lookup helper that raises HTTPException(404) keeps every route's "not found" identical.
  • model_dump(exclude_none=True) plus setattr updates only the fields the client sent.
  • Set status_code for 201 and 204. A 204 route returns nothing.
  • Send JSON with curl using -H "Content-Type: application/json" --data "@file.json".
  • Tests with TestClient need no server. Reset shared state in setUp, and use ids from responses.

  • Give the app a description: FastAPI(title="Notes API", description="...", version="1.0.0"), then look at /docs.

  • FastAPI: Body - Updates (opens in a new tab): the official take on partial updates with exclude_unset.

What you'll learn

  • Add routes to a FastAPI app without breaking existing ones, including fixed paths next to {param} paths.
  • Set response headers and choose between 201, 204, 404, 409, and 422.
  • Explain the difference between PUT and PATCH by implementing both.

Each exercise adds one feature to the notes API from the last lesson. Write your answer in notes-api/main.py, check it with TestClient (in test_main.py, or a scratch file), then compare with the solution.

All cells on this page share one Python session. The starter below is the finished app from the last lesson, plus two helpers: reset() empties the store and restarts ids at 1, and add() puts a note straight into the list so exercises can start with data. To keep each solution easy to read, it builds a fresh small app containing only the routes that exercise is about.

#Warm-up: a health check

Add GET /health that returns {"status": "ok"}. Servers in production get asked this every few seconds by monitoring tools, so it should be fast and depend on nothing.

Show solution

#Exercise 1: Count the notes

Add GET /notes/count, which returns {"count": n} and accepts the same q filter as the list. Make sure GET /notes/1 still works afterwards.

Need a hint?

Remember the route-order trap from the Notes lesson. Which has to come first in the file, /notes/count or /notes/{note_id}? Test both URLs to be sure.

Show solution

/notes/count is declared first. The other way round, count would be read as a note_id and fail the int check with a 422. In your main.py, put count_notes above get_note. Copying the filter line from list_notes works, but if the two ever drift apart, the count and the list will disagree; pulling the filter into a small matching(q) helper fixes that for good.

#Exercise 2: Say where the new note lives

201 Created responses traditionally include a Location header with the new resource's URL. Make POST /notes send Location: /notes/{id}.

Need a hint?

Add a parameter response: Response to the route function. FastAPI fills it in, and anything you put in response.headers is sent along with your return value.

Show solution

A client can now follow the header instead of building the URL itself. That matters more than it seems: if you later move notes to /v2/notes/{id}, clients that follow Location keep working.

#Exercise 3: PUT replaces, PATCH changes

Add PUT /notes/{note_id}, which replaces the whole note with a NoteIn body. Then show the difference: start with {"title": "Buy milk", "body": "2 cartons"}, send {"title": "Buy oat milk"} with PATCH to one copy and with PUT to another, and print both results.

Need a hint?

PUT's body is a complete note, so use NoteIn, not NoteUpdate. A field the client leaves out takes its default, which for body is "". Keep the same id.

Show solution

Same body, different meaning. PATCH says "change these fields", so the body survives. PUT says "here is the whole note", so the missing body becomes the default. PUT also requires title, which is why the last request gets a 422. PUT is idempotent (sending it twice leaves the same note), which makes it safe for a client to retry.

#Exercise 4: Refuse duplicate titles

Make POST /notes answer 409 Conflict with {"detail": "A note titled 'Buy milk' already exists"} if a note with the same title exists, ignoring case.

Need a hint?

Check before creating anything: any(...) over the existing notes, comparing .lower() of both titles. Raise, don't return. Use the title the client sent in the message.

Show solution

409 is right because "BUY MILK" is a perfectly valid title on its own (so not 422); it only clashes with what's stored. A complete version would also check PATCH and PUT, since renaming a note to an existing title is the same conflict through a different door. Also notice the failed attempt didn't use up an id: "Buy bread" got 2, because the check runs before next(ids).

#Exercise 5: A versioned list with a total

A client wants to show "Page 2 of 5", which needs a total count. Changing GET /notes to return an object would break every existing client, so add GET /v2/notes that returns {"items": [...], "total": n, "limit": ..., "offset": ...}, and leave GET /notes exactly as it is.

What you'll learn

  • Explain why storing the same fact in many rows leads to contradictions.
  • Create SQLite tables with primary keys, foreign keys, and NOT NULL/UNIQUE rules.
  • Filter and sort rows with WHERE and ORDER BY.
  • Combine tables with JOIN and LEFT JOIN, and count with GROUP BY.

The robotics club keeps its sign-ups in one table: event, date, member name, member email. Maya changes her email address. The organizer fixes the row for the Hackathon, the one on screen, and moves on. Now ask the table for Maya's email:

Maya now has two email addresses, and nothing in the data says which one is real. Nobody typed anything wrong. The table's shape caused it: her email was stored twice, so it could change in one place and not the other. The same shape causes two more bugs. A new member who hasn't signed up for anything has no row to live in, and deleting the last sign-up for an event deletes every trace that the event exists.

The fix is a rule database designers call normalization, and the plain-words version is short: store each fact once, in the table about that thing. Maya's email is a fact about Maya, so it belongs in a members table. The Hackathon's date is a fact about the Hackathon. "Maya is going to the Hackathon" is a fact about a sign-up, and that table only needs to point at the other two.

#A table per kind of thing, a primary key per row

A relational database is a set of tables. Each table holds one kind of thing, each row is one of those things, and each column is one property with a type. Every row gets a primary key: a value that identifies it and never changes, even when the name or email does.

In SQLite, a column declared INTEGER PRIMARY KEY is filled in for you with 1, 2, 3, and so on. This program saves the club as three tables in a file called club.db, then asks a question with WHERE (which rows) and ORDER BY (in what order):

Three things to notice. NOT NULL refuses a missing value and UNIQUE refuses a second member with the same email, so the database itself enforces rules your Python might forget. Dates are stored as 'YYYY-MM-DD' text, which sorts and compares correctly as plain strings. And Sam is in the members table even though he hasn't signed up for anything, which the flat table couldn't do.

#Foreign keys point at a row in another table

The signups table holds only two numbers per row. member_id is a foreign key: it must match the id of some row in members. The pair (member_id, event_id) is the table's primary key, so Maya can't sign up for the same event twice.

Read ||--o{ as "one to zero-or-more": one member makes any number of sign-ups. A member who goes to many events and an event with many members is a many-to-many relationship, and a linking table like signups is how every relational database stores one.

There's a catch that surprises almost everyone the first time:

SQLite keeps foreign key checks off unless each connection turns them on with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON. The first insert pointed at a member who doesn't exist and was accepted anyway. After the pragma, the same insert fails with FOREIGN KEY constraint failed. Most other databases check foreign keys by default; with SQLite, put that pragma right after every connect.

#JOIN puts the pieces back together

Splitting the data was the easy part. Now you need "who is going to what" as readable names again. Here's the intuition before the SQL: for each sign-up, look up the member with that id and the event with that id, and glue the results into one row.

That loop is what a JOIN describes. You write the matching rule after ON, and the database works out how to do the lookups. Because Maya's email now lives in one row, changing it once changes it everywhere it shows up:

Both of Maya's rows show the new address. A plain JOIN (also spelled INNER JOIN) keeps only rows that found a match, which is why Sam and the Field trip are missing: no sign-up mentions them.

#LEFT JOIN and GROUP BY answer "how many?"

The organizer wants a head count for every event, including events nobody has signed up for yet. LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the table on the left (events), filling the sign-up columns with NULL when there's no match. GROUP BY then squashes the rows for each event into one, and COUNT counts them.

The Field trip shows 0 going, which is right. The second query says 1, which is wrong, and the reason is subtle: COUNT(*) counts rows, and the LEFT JOIN produced one row for the Field trip (with NULL sign-up columns). COUNT(signups.member_id) counts only non-NULL values. To keep only some groups, add HAVING after GROUP BY, for example HAVING going >= 2. WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters the groups after.

⚠️ Watch out

Three bugs almost everyone meets in their first days of SQL.

  1. Foreign keys silently unchecked. Without PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, SQLite accepts a sign-up for member 99. Run the pragma after every connect.
  2. COUNT(*) after a LEFT JOIN reports 1 for an empty group. Count a column from the right-hand table instead.
  3. sqlite3.OperationalError: ambiguous column name: name. Both members and events have a name column, so SELECT name ... JOIN ... can't tell which one you mean. Write members.name or events.name.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A new member, Ana, joins the club but hasn't signed up for an event. In the three-table design, where does her email go?

  • That was the flat table's problem. The members table holds members whether or not they have sign-ups.

  • Her email is a fact about her, so it's stored once in the table about members.

  • event_id is NOT NULL and a foreign key, so that row would be rejected, and it would mix two kinds of facts anyway.

Show answer

B. Her email is a fact about her, so it's stored once in the table about members.

2You run SELECT events.name, COUNT(*) FROM events LEFT JOIN signups ON signups.event_id = events.id GROUP BY events.id. What does it report for an event with no sign-ups?

  • That's what you want, but COUNT(*) counts the single row the LEFT JOIN created for the event.

  • The unmatched event still produces one row (with NULL sign-up columns), and COUNT(*) counts rows.

  • A plain JOIN would leave it out. LEFT JOIN keeps every event.

Show answer

B. The unmatched event still produces one row (with NULL sign-up columns), and COUNT(*) counts rows.

3Which query lists every member, including members with no sign-ups?

  • An inner join drops members who have no matching sign-up row.

  • LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, members, matched or not.

  • This keeps every sign-up, not every member. Sam still wouldn't appear.

Show answer

B. LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, members, matched or not.

4A program inserts (member_id=99, event_id=1) into signups on a fresh connection and no error appears. Why?

  • They check both, once they're switched on.

  • Databases never invent the parent row for you.

  • SQLite leaves foreign key enforcement off per connection unless you turn it on.

Show answer

C. SQLite leaves foreign key enforcement off per connection unless you turn it on.

Key takeaways

  • Store each fact once, in the table about that thing. Repeated facts drift apart.
  • A primary key identifies a row forever; a foreign key stores another row's primary key.
  • Many-to-many relationships get their own linking table, like signups.
  • JOIN ... ON reassembles related rows; LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched rows from the left table.
  • GROUP BY with COUNT(column) gives per-group totals, and HAVING filters the groups.
  • In SQLite, run PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON on every connection.

#Further reading

  • SQLite: the SELECT statement (opens in a new tab), the official reference for joins, GROUP BY, HAVING, and ORDER BY, with railroad diagrams of the grammar.
  • SQLite foreign key support (opens in a new tab) explains why enforcement is off by default and what ON DELETE CASCADE does.
  • Python's sqlite3 module (opens in a new tab), with a tutorial at the top and the full API for connections, cursors, and transactions below it.

m5-l2.html:
What you'll learn

  • Turn an app's data into a schema with users, notes, tags, and a linking table.
  • Write the queries an API needs as small Python functions that return dictionaries.
  • Use commit, rowcount, and ON DELETE CASCADE correctly.
  • Read EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN to see an index working.
  • Group several writes into one transaction with with conn:.

The notes API from earlier modules keeps its notes in a Python list. Restart the server and every note is gone. In this build you'll make the database that replaces that list: a file called notes.db that survives restarts, knows which user owns each note, and lets notes carry tags like school or health.

Here is the finished design. Every cell in this lesson shares one Python session, like a notebook, so each step builds on the one before. On your computer, put the cells one after another in a single file and run it.

#Step 1: Create the tables

A schema is a contract the database enforces for you. The interesting parts here are the rules on the columns. CHECK (length(title) BETWEEN 1 AND 100) refuses blank or huge titles even if a bug in your Python lets one through. DEFAULT (datetime('now')) stamps new notes with the current UTC time. ON DELETE CASCADE says "when the parent row is deleted, delete the rows that point at it", so deleting a note also deletes its tag links.

sqlite_master is SQLite's own table of contents, so querying it confirms all four tables exist. IF NOT EXISTS makes the script safe to run twice.

#Step 2: Add seed data, and see what commit does

Seed data is a small, realistic set of rows to develop against. executemany runs one INSERT once per tuple. The timestamps are typed out so that "newest first" has a predictable answer.

Python's sqlite3 starts a transaction before the first INSERT, and nothing is permanent until commit(). The second connection plays the part of a second request to your API: until the commit, it sees zero notes. Forget commit() in a route and the API will report success while saving nothing.

#Step 3: Write the reads the API will need

Each API route will need one query. Writing them as functions now means the routes in a later module stay short. Setting conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row makes each row behave like a dictionary, so dict(row) turns it into exactly the JSON-ready shape a FastAPI route can return.

LIMIT ? caps the result, which is how an API pages through long lists. Every value from outside the function goes in through a ? placeholder, never pasted into the SQL string. Module 6 shows exactly what goes wrong if you paste.

#Step 4: Update and delete only what the user owns

The ownership check can live inside the SQL. WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ? matches nothing if the note belongs to someone else, and cursor.rowcount tells you how many rows changed. Zero means "not found, or not yours", which the API will turn into an error response.

Note 3 had two tags, and both links vanished with it. That's the cascade doing its job, and it only works because step 1 turned on PRAGMA foreign_keys.

#Step 5: Add an index for the most common query

Every time Ana opens the app, the API runs "Ana's notes, newest first". Without help, SQLite reads every row in notes to find hers, then sorts them. An index is a sorted copy of some columns with pointers back to the rows, like the index at the back of a textbook. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows which strategy SQLite picked.

SCAN notes means "read the whole table", and USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY means "then sort". With the index it becomes SEARCH ... USING INDEX: jump straight to Ana's entries, already in date order. With four notes you won't feel the difference; with a million, it's the difference between milliseconds and seconds. Indexes cost disk space and slow down writes a little, so add them for queries you run constantly, not for every column.

#Step 6: Save a note and its tags in one transaction

Creating a tagged note takes several statements: insert the note, make sure each tag exists, link them. If the third statement fails, you'd be left with a note missing its tags. A transaction makes the whole group all-or-nothing. Used as with conn:, a connection commits when the block finishes and rolls everything back if an exception escapes it.

The second call inserted "Packing list" and the travel tag before the long tag broke the CHECK rule. The rollback erased both: the note count stayed at 4 and travel never appears in the tag counts. ON CONFLICT (name) DO NOTHING reuses a tag that already exists, such as health.

⚠️ Watch out

INSERT OR IGNORE looks like a shortcut for "skip it if the tag exists", but it also skips rows that break NOT NULL and CHECK rules, silently. Here the long tag would vanish without an error and the next line would crash on None. ON CONFLICT (name) DO NOTHING only ignores the duplicate-name case.

#The finished program

Here is everything in one file. It rebuilds notes.db from the seed data each run, which is what you want while developing.

The "Bio flashcards" note has no typed-out timestamp, so its created_at comes from the clock and it sorts to the top as the newest note.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does note_tags use PRIMARY KEY (note_id, tag_id) instead of its own id column?

  • It doesn't; you could add more columns, such as when the tag was added.

  • A composite primary key makes the combination the identity of the row and blocks duplicates.

  • Cascades come from the REFERENCES ... ON DELETE CASCADE clauses, not from the primary key.

Show answer

B. A composite primary key makes the combination the identity of the row and blocks duplicates.

2rename_note(conn, 2, user_id=2, title="Hacked") returned False. What did the database actually do?

  • No exception happened. The UPDATE ran successfully and matched no rows.

  • rowcount was 0, so the function reported that nothing changed.

  • The WHERE clause excluded the row before anything changed.

Show answer

B. rowcount was 0, so the function reported that nothing changed.

3Why is the index on (user_id, created_at) rather than only (user_id)?

  • Indexes can be on any columns.

  • They use more, if anything.

  • The second column keeps each user's entries sorted by time, which removed the temp B-tree step.

Show answer

C. The second column keeps each user's entries sorted by time, which removed the temp B-tree step.

Key takeaways

  • Write the schema's rules (NOT NULL, UNIQUE, CHECK, foreign keys) into the database so they hold even when application code slips.
  • Nothing is saved until commit(). with conn: commits for you, or rolls back on an exception.
  • Put ownership into the WHERE clause and check rowcount to see whether anything matched.
  • ON DELETE CASCADE removes dependent rows, but only with PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON.
  • Index the columns your most frequent query filters and sorts by, and confirm with EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN.

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add a pinned INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (pinned IN (0, 1)) column and change notes_for so pinned notes come first.
  • Write remove_tag(conn, note_id, tag_name) and a query that finds tags no note uses any more.
  • Add a search_notes(conn, user_id, text) that matches titles with LIKE, passing '%' + text + '%' as the parameter.

#Further reading

  • The SQLite query planner (opens in a new tab) explains with pictures how indexes turn a full scan into a quick search, and why column order in an index matters.
  • SQLite: transactions (opens in a new tab) covers BEGIN, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK and the locking behavior behind them.
  • SQLite UPSERT (opens in a new tab) documents ON CONFLICT ... DO NOTHING and DO UPDATE.

m5-l3.html:
What you'll learn

  • Write WHERE/ORDER BY filters and multi-table joins from a plain-English request.
  • Find missing matches with LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL.
  • Summarize with GROUP BY and HAVING.
  • Design a many-to-many table and a transaction that keeps two tables consistent.

Every exercise uses the same small school library. Run the setup program once; it writes library.db next to it, and each solution opens that file. Exercises 5 and 6 change the database, so if you want to start over, delete library.db and run the setup again.

#Warm-up: predict the order

Before running it, write down what this prints: SELECT title FROM books WHERE year < 1990 ORDER BY year DESC.

WHERE keeps the three older books, then DESC puts the largest year (1987) first. Each row comes back as a tuple, which is why every title sits inside its own parentheses.

#Exercise 1: Recent books, newest first

Print the title and year of every book published in 2000 or later, newest first.

Need a hint?

One WHERE with >=, then ORDER BY the same column with DESC. Select only the two columns you need.

Show solution

>= 2000 includes the boundary year. Asking for title, year instead of * keeps the output to what the request asked for, which is also what an API response should do.

#Exercise 2: Who has which book right now?

List every loan that hasn't been returned, as (student name, book title, borrowed date), oldest loan first.

Need a hint?

Start FROM loans and join students and books to it. An unreturned loan has returned_on set to NULL, and returned_on = NULL is never true, not even for NULL. SQL has a special operator for this test.

Show solution

NULL means "unknown", and comparing anything to unknown gives unknown, so = NULL matches nothing. IS NULL is the test that works.

#Exercise 3: Never borrowed

Print the titles of books that have never been borrowed, then the names of students who have never borrowed anything.

Need a hint?

A LEFT JOIN from books to loans keeps every book. For a book with no loans, every loans column in that row is NULL. Filter on one of them.

Show solution

This "anti-join" pattern answers every "which X has no Y?" question. Test a column that can never be NULL in a real match, like the primary key loans.id.

#Exercise 4: Frequent borrowers

For each student with two or more loans in total, print their name, total loans, and how many are still out. Sort by total, highest first, then by name.

Need a hint?

GROUP BY students.id, COUNT(loans.id) for the total, and HAVING for the "two or more" rule. In SQLite a comparison like returned_on IS NULL evaluates to 1 or 0, so you can add it up with SUM.

Show solution

HAVING runs after the groups are built, so it can use the total alias. A WHERE total >= 2 would fail, because WHERE runs on single rows before any counting happens.

#Exercise 5: Design the clubs feature

The library runs reading clubs, and a student can join any number of them. Add clubs and club_members tables, put Ava, Jonah, and Tariq in the Sci-fi club and Mei and Ava in the Poetry club, and create an empty Manga club. Show that adding Jonah to the Sci-fi club a second time is rejected, then print every club with its member count.

Need a hint?

This is many-to-many, so it needs a linking table with two foreign keys. Making the pair of columns the primary key is what rejects the duplicate. For the counts, remember the COUNT(*) trap with LEFT JOIN.

Show solution

The error names both columns because the uniqueness rule covers the pair. Ava appears in two clubs, which is fine: only the same pair twice is refused.

#Exercise 6: A checkout that can't half-happen

Write checkout(conn, book_id, student_id, day) that adds a loan and lowers that book's copies_available by one. If either step fails, neither should stick. Check out Hatchet (book 3) for Tariq (student 4), then try Dune (book 2), which has no copies left.

Need a hint?

Do the INSERT first and the UPDATE second, inside one with conn: block. The CHECK (copies_available >= 0) rule from the setup refuses the update, and the block has to undo the insert that already ran.

Show solution

The loan count stayed at 8 after the Dune attempt, so the inserted loan was rolled back with the failed update. Without with conn: (and with a commit() after each statement), the library would record a loan for a book it doesn't have. Notice also that copies_available - 1 is computed inside SQL, so two checkouts at once can't both read "1" and both write "0".

#Challenge: Normalize a flat order sheet with SQL alone

The school store logged orders in one table that repeats each customer's email and each product's price on every line. Split it into customers, products, orders, and order_lines using only INSERT INTO ... SELECT (no Python loops). Then prove nothing was lost: a join across the new tables should give back exactly the original rows.

Need a hint?

SELECT DISTINCT customer, email FROM flat_orders gives one row per customer. To fill orders and order_lines, join flat_orders to the new tables on a column that's unique there (email for customers, name for products) to look up the new ids. SQL's EXCEPT returns rows in the first query that aren't in the second; try it in both directions.

Show solution

Ava's email is now stored once instead of three times, and the Notebook's price once instead of twice. Two empty EXCEPT results in both directions mean the new design holds exactly the same information as the old one. This is a real technique: migrations that restructure a live database usually end with a check like this one.

m6-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Reject malformed requests with Pydantic field rules and read the 422 errors they produce.
  • Explain SQL injection from a real vulnerable query, and prevent it with placeholders.
  • Hash and verify passwords with hashlib.scrypt, a random salt, and hmac.compare_digest.
  • Tell authentication (401) from authorization (403) and check ownership on every write.
  • Describe what CORS and rate limits protect, and what they don't.

Ben logs in to the notes app, sends PATCH /notes/7, and changes the title of Ana's diary entry. Nobody stole a password. The server checked "is someone logged in?" and never asked "is note 7 theirs?"

A server can't trust anything in a request: not the body, not the URL, not the claim of who sent it. So each request passes a series of checks at the boundary, the point where outside data enters your code, and each failed check has its own status code.

#Pydantic checks the shape before your code runs

A FastAPI route that takes a Pydantic model never sees a request that breaks the model's rules. Field adds limits on top of the type, and extra="forbid" rejects keys you didn't ask for.

Look at the fourth attempt: a client tried to set owner_id itself, hoping the server would save whatever it sent. Without extra="forbid" Pydantic would silently drop the key; forbidding it tells the client the request was wrong. The last attempt shows Pydantic converting the string "2" to the integer 2; add strict=True to a Field to refuse that.

Validation answers "is this well-formed?" It does not make data safe to paste into SQL or HTML. A perfectly valid title can still be an attack.

#SQL injection: when a value turns into code

Here's a function that looks up notes by owner by gluing the owner's name into the SQL text with an f-string:

The second "name" contains a quote that closes the string early, so the rest, OR '1'='1', becomes part of the query's logic. That's true for every row, so the attacker gets everyone's notes. The database did what it was told; the bug is that user data became SQL code.

The fix is the ? placeholder you've used since the last module. The SQL text and the values travel to SQLite separately, so a value can never be read as code:

The attack string is now just an odd name that matches nobody. Placeholders work for values only. If a user chooses a column to sort by, you can't write ORDER BY ?; check their choice against a fixed set of allowed names instead.

#Store a password so a stolen database doesn't reveal it

Databases leak through misplaced backups, bugs, and stolen laptops. If passwords are stored as typed, every account is exposed, along with every other site where people reused them. So servers store a hash, the output of a one-way function, and at login they hash what was typed and compare.

Two details matter. A salt (random bytes stored next to the hash) makes the same password hash differently for every user, so an attacker can't crack everyone at once with a precomputed table. And the hash must be slow. A general-purpose hash like SHA-256 is built for speed, which helps an attacker try billions of guesses. scrypt is deliberately slow and memory-hungry.

Same password, two different stored strings, because each got its own salt. secrets (not random) generates the salt, since random is predictable by design. hmac.compare_digest compares in constant time, so response timing doesn't hint at how many characters matched.

📝 Note

n=2**14 keeps this course's tests quick. The OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet currently recommends at least n=2**17 for scrypt; at that size you also need to pass maxmem=2**28, because Python's default memory cap is too small for it.

#Authentication asks who; authorization asks whether

Authentication proves who is sending the request. After a correct password, the server creates a random token with secrets.token_urlsafe(32), remembers which user it belongs to, and gives it to the client. The client sends it back on every request in a header: Authorization: Bearer <token>.

Authorization decides whether this user may do this action to this record. It's a separate check, and it has to happen on every route that reads or changes something private. This app has the buggy route from the opening next to a fixed one:

The buggy route let Ben rewrite Ana's note. The fixed one gives 401 with no token ("who are you?") and 403 for Ben ("I know who you are, and no"). Some APIs answer 404 instead, so outsiders can't even learn that note 7 exists.

#CORS and rate limits: two rules people mix up

CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is enforced by browsers. By default, JavaScript on one origin, such as https://notes-frontend.example, can't read responses from a different origin, such as your API. The API opts in by sending an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header, which FastAPI's middleware adds for the origins you list:

CORS protects people's browsers from other websites; it does not protect your API. Scripts and curl ignore it completely. If the page and the API share an origin, you don't need CORS at all.

A rate limit caps how many requests one client (an IP address, an account) can make per time window, say 5 login attempts a minute. Past the limit the server answers 429 Too Many Requests, often with a Retry-After header giving the seconds to wait. That shrinks a password-guessing attack from millions of tries a day to a handful. In production it usually lives in a reverse proxy, the hosting platform, or a library; you'll write a small one in the practice lesson.

⚠️ Watch out

Classic mistakes at the boundary.

  • Building SQL with f-strings or +. Even "trusted" values like usernames can contain quotes.
  • Checking login but not ownership. Every route with a record id in the URL needs the ownership check.
  • Hashing with plain hashlib.sha256(password): fast and unsalted means crackable.
  • "Fixing" a CORS error with allow_origins=["*"] and assuming the API is now protected.

Check your understanding

4 questions

1A search route runs f"SELECT title FROM notes WHERE title LIKE '%{term}%' AND owner = 'ana'". Someone searches for %' --. What happens?

  • Any value pasted into SQL text can change the query.

  • The rest of the line becomes a comment, so the AND owner = 'ana' filter disappears.

  • The resulting SQL is valid; attackers craft it to be.

Show answer

B. The rest of the line becomes a comment, so the AND owner = 'ana' filter disappears.

2Ben sends a valid token and asks to delete Ana's note. Which status best describes the refusal?

  • 401 means "we don't know who you are". The token proved he's Ben.

  • He's authenticated but not authorized for this record.

  • 422 is for malformed input. His request was well-formed.

Show answer

B. He's authenticated but not authorized for this record.

3Why does each user's password get its own random salt?

  • A salt makes every hash unique, forcing an attacker to crack each account separately.

  • Hashing is one-way; there is nothing to decrypt.

  • The salt doesn't change speed. Slowness comes from the n, r, and p settings.

Show answer

A. A salt makes every hash unique, forcing an attacker to crack each account separately.

4Your teammate says "We set CORS to only allow our frontend, so nobody else can call our API." What's wrong?

  • CORS only controls what browsers let other pages read.

  • CORS protects users' browsers from other websites, not your server from direct requests.

  • It applies to all methods; some requests even get a preflight OPTIONS check.

Show answer

B. CORS protects users' browsers from other websites, not your server from direct requests.

Key takeaways

  • Check every request at the boundary: shape (422), identity (401), permission (403), then run the action.
  • Pydantic Field limits and extra="forbid" stop malformed and over-posted data before your code runs.
  • Never build SQL from strings. ? placeholders keep values from becoming code.
  • Store salted, slow hashes (scrypt, pbkdf2_hmac) and compare with hmac.compare_digest.
  • Logged in is not the same as allowed: check ownership on every route that touches a private record.
  • CORS is a browser rule for reading responses; rate limits slow down guessing. Neither replaces authorization.

  • OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet (opens in a new tab), the standard reference on parameterized queries and allow-listing.
  • OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet (opens in a new tab) lists current recommended settings for Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt, and PBKDF2.
  • MDN: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (opens in a new tab) explains origins, preflight requests, and every Access-Control-* header.

What you'll learn

  • Validate sign-up and note data with strict Pydantic models.
  • Store passwords as salted scrypt hashes and issue random bearer tokens at login.
  • Write a current_user dependency that turns a missing or bad token into a 401.
  • Return 403 when someone touches a note they don't own, and test that it happens.

Right now anyone who can reach the notes API can read and rewrite every note. By the end of this build, each note has an owner, and the API enforces the rules in this table. Every row with "yes" in the token column goes through the same dependency, so the rule can't be forgotten on one route.

Method and path Token needed? Success Failures
POST /signup no 201 409 name taken, 422 bad input
POST /login no 200 with a token 401 wrong name or password
GET /me yes 200 401
POST /notes yes 201 401, 422
GET /notes yes 200, only your notes 401
PATCH /notes/{id} yes 200 401, 403 not yours, 404, 422
DELETE /notes/{id} yes 204 401, 403, 404

The cells below share one Python session, so each step uses what the earlier ones defined. In your project, steps 1 to 5 all go in notes-api/main.py, and step 6 goes in notes-api/test_main.py. Data stays in dictionaries for now; the next module moves it into SQLite.

#Step 1: Models that say exactly what's allowed

Usernames become part of URLs and log lines, so keep them boring: 3 to 20 lowercase letters, digits, or underscores. Passwords get a minimum length and nothing else, because rules like "must contain a symbol" mostly produce Password1!. NoteIn has no owner field at all: the owner comes from the token, never from the request body.

Calling a model directly, without FastAPI, is a quick way to try its rules. Both problems with the second sign-up are reported at once, which is what the API's 422 response will do too.

#Step 2: Hash passwords before they touch storage

The stored string starts with scrypt$ so that a future version of your app can tell which algorithm made it, and switch to a stronger one without breaking old accounts. The salt and the hash travel together, separated by $.

One capital letter is enough to fail, as it should be. Nothing in the stored string can be turned back into the password; the only way to check a guess is to hash it again.

#Step 3: Sign up and log in

Sign-up hashes and stores. Login looks the user up, verifies, and hands out a fresh random token. The server keeps a tokens dictionary mapping each token to its username, which is how a later request proves who it's from.

The failed login says "wrong username or password" without saying which. Telling an attacker "no such user" would let them test a list of names first. token_urlsafe(32) uses 32 random bytes, far too many to guess, encoded as 43 URL-safe characters.

#Step 4: A dependency that answers "who is this?"

A FastAPI dependency is a function the framework calls before your route, passing its return value in as a parameter. current_user reads the Authorization header, splits Bearer <token>, and either returns a username or stops the request with a 401.

The parameter is named authorization and FastAPI maps it to the Authorization header for you. The WWW-Authenticate: Bearer header on a 401 is the HTTP standard's way of saying which kind of credentials to send.

#Step 5: Notes that belong to someone

Every note route takes user: str = Depends(current_user). The helper owned_note does the 404 and 403 checks in one place, so edit and delete can't drift apart. response_model=NoteOut makes FastAPI filter the output to exactly those fields.

Ben's edit and delete both bounced with 403, and Ana's note is untouched. GET /notes filters by owner too: a list route that returned everyone's notes would leak just as badly as an unchecked edit.

#Step 6: Tests that lock the rules in

Security rules are easy to break later by accident, so each one gets a test. setUpClass creates the two accounts once (hashing is slow on purpose, so you don't want to repeat it), and setUp empties the notes before every test so tests can't leak state into each other.

Run the tests from the notes-api folder with python -m unittest. (Leave out the last two lines in your file; they're how this page runs the tests.) The test that matters most is test_other_user_cannot_edit_or_delete: it's the bug from the start of this module, written down so it can never come back unnoticed.

#The finished main.py

Start it with fastapi dev main.py, then try the flow by hand from your client terminal. Log in, copy the token from the response, and send it back:

The tokens live in a dictionary, so restarting the server (which fastapi dev does every time you save) logs everyone out. Storing users and tokens in SQLite, next module, fixes that.

3 questions

1Why does NoteIn have no owner field, when every saved note has one?

  • It can, as Credentials shows. The issue is who gets to decide the value.

  • If the body could set owner, anyone could create or move notes into someone else's account.

  • Size has nothing to do with it; this is about trust.

Show answer

B. If the body could set owner, anyone could create or move notes into someone else's account.

2Why is the ownership check in a helper, owned_note, instead of written inline in each route?

  • It doesn't; inline checks work, they're just easy to get inconsistent.

  • One function, one rule. Copies of a security check tend to drift apart.

  • The speed is the same. This is about keeping the rule in one place.

Show answer

B. One function, one rule. Copies of a security check tend to drift apart.

3Login fails. Why does the API say "Wrong username or password" instead of "No user named ana"?

  • It does know. It chooses not to say.

  • A vague message gives away less. (Sign-up still reveals taken names, a trade-off most apps accept.)

  • The status code is standard; the message text is up to you.

Key takeaways

  • The owner of a record comes from the token, never from the request body. extra="forbid" rejects attempts to sneak it in.
  • Store scrypt$salt$hash, verify with hmac.compare_digest, and give the same error for unknown users and wrong passwords.
  • secrets.token_urlsafe(32) makes an unguessable bearer token; a current_user dependency turns it back into a username or a 401.
  • Put the 404 and 403 checks in one helper and call it from every route that touches a single record.
  • Write a test for each security rule, especially "another user can't edit or delete my record".

#Ideas to extend it

  • Add POST /logout that deletes the caller's token from tokens, and a test that the old token then gets 401.
  • Give tokens an expiry: store (username, expires_at) and reject tokens older than an hour.
  • Store hashlib.sha256(token.encode()).hexdigest() as the dictionary key instead of the raw token, so a leaked token table can't be used directly.

What you'll learn

  • Write Pydantic rules for a real form and predict which payloads fail.
  • Fix SQL injection in a LIKE search and in a user-chosen sort order.
  • Store and verify PBKDF2 password hashes that record their own settings.
  • Express an authorization rule as a function and test it case by case.
  • Return 429 with Retry-After from a login route, and check CORS preflight responses.

#Warm-up: name the status code

For each request to the notes API from the last lesson, decide which status comes back before reading the answers.

  1. POST /notes with a valid token and {"title": ""}.
  2. PATCH /notes/4 with no Authorization header.
  3. DELETE /notes/4 with Ben's token, where note 4 is Ana's.
  4. PATCH /notes/999 with Ana's token, where no note 999 exists.
  5. The sixth wrong password for ana within a minute, on an API with a 5-per-minute limit.
Show solution
  1. 422: the body fails min_length=1. FastAPI validates the body before your code runs.
  2. 401: nobody is identified, so permission can't even be asked.
  3. 403 (or 404 if the API hides other people's records): Ben is known but not allowed.
  4. 404: Ana is allowed to look, and there's nothing there.
  5. 429: the limiter refuses before the password is even checked.

#Exercise 1: Validate an event sign-up form

The club's sign-up form sends name, grade (6 to 12), email, shirt (S, M, L, or XL), and optional guests (0 to 2). Write an EventSignup model that rejects blank names (even all spaces), unknown keys, and anything outside those ranges, then run these five payloads through it.

Need a hint?

Literal["S", "M", "L", "XL"] from typing limits a field to fixed choices. str_strip_whitespace=True in the ConfigDict trims spaces before min_length is checked, which is what catches " ".

Show solution

The email pattern only checks the rough shape (something, @, something, dot, letters). That's as far as validation should go; the only real proof that an address works is sending it a message. Pydantic also has an EmailStr type, which needs the separate email-validator package.

#Exercise 2: Close the hole in a search box

This search was meant to find Ana's notes whose title contains a word. Show that searching for %' -- leaks Ben's notes, then fix it so the same input finds nothing.

Need a hint?

The % wildcards can't sit inside the quotes around a ?. Either build the pattern in Python and pass f"%{term}%" as the parameter, or let SQL glue it together with '%' || ? || '%' (|| joins strings in SQL).

Show solution

In the unsafe version, -- starts an SQL comment, so AND owner = 'ana' is thrown away. With placeholders the attack text is only a search term, and no title contains it.

#Exercise 3: Let users choose the sort order, safely

GET /books?sort=year should sort by the column the user picks. Write list_books(sort) that accepts title, year, or newest, and refuses anything else, including year; DROP TABLE books.

Need a hint?

ORDER BY ? runs without an error but sorts by the constant text 'year', which means not sorting at all. Placeholders only stand in for values. Map each allowed choice to a piece of SQL you wrote yourself, in a dictionary.

Show solution

The f-string is safe here only because every possible value comes from SORTABLE, text you wrote. In a FastAPI route, sort: Literal["title", "year", "newest"] = "title" gives the same protection and a 422 for anything else.

#Exercise 4: Password hashes that can be upgraded

Write hash_password and verify_password with hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac and SHA-256. The stored string must record the algorithm and iteration count, as pbkdf2_sha256$600000$<salt>$<hash>, so an old hash made with fewer iterations still verifies. Add needs_rehash(stored) that says when a hash is weaker than today's setting.

Need a hint?

verify_password must read the iteration count out of the stored string, not use the current constant. pbkdf2_hmac(name, password_bytes, salt, iterations) takes the algorithm name as a string.

Show solution

The upgrade happens at login, the only moment the server sees the real password: if it verifies and needs_rehash is true, hash it again with today's setting and save the new string.

#Exercise 5: Write the permission rule as a function

On the club's message board, members can edit their own posts and organizers can edit any post, but nobody can edit a post once its event is archived. Write can_edit(user, post) and check it against every combination below.

Need a hint?

Check the rule that overrides everything (archived) first, then the role, then ownership. Writing the expected answers down as a list of (user, post, expected) tuples before writing the function is how you catch a rule in the wrong order.

Show solution

Swap the first two if blocks and the last case fails: the organizer could edit an archived post. Keeping the rule in one plain function makes it testable without any HTTP at all; routes call it and raise 403 when it says no.

#Exercise 6: Rate-limit the login route

Write a FixedWindowLimiter that allows limit attempts per window seconds for each key, and use it in a /login route keyed by username. The sixth attempt in a minute gets 429 with a Retry-After header. Pass the limiter a fake clock so the test can jump forward in time instead of sleeping.

Need a hint?

Store (window_start, count) per key. On each hit: if the window has expired, start a new one with count 0; if the count has reached the limit, refuse and report ceil(window_start + window - now) seconds; otherwise add one. Check the limiter before checking the password, so blocked guesses cost the server nothing.

Show solution

Even the right password is refused 30 seconds in, because the window hasn't ended. Keying only by username has a downside: anyone can lock Ana out by guessing wrong on purpose. Real systems combine a per-account limit with a per-IP limit (FastAPI gives you the caller's address as request.client.host), and keep the counts somewhere shared, such as a database, when there's more than one server process.

#Challenge: Prove your CORS setup does what you think

Your page runs at http://localhost:5500 and calls the API with PATCH and an Authorization header. Configure CORSMiddleware for exactly that, then use TestClient to send the preflight request a browser sends first (OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method headers). Check three preflights (your origin, a stranger's origin, and your origin asking for PUT), then send a plain GET from the stranger's origin and look closely at whether the route ran.

Need a hint?

A preflight is client.options("/notes", headers={"Origin": ..., "Access-Control-Request-Method": "PATCH", "Access-Control-Request-Headers": "authorization"}). Print the status, the access-control-allow-origin response header, and the body. For the GET, keep a list that the route appends to, so you can see whether it ran.

Show solution

The last line is the lesson. The stranger's GET got a 200, the route ran, and the data came back; the only difference is the missing access-control-allow-origin header. A browser would see that and refuse to hand the response to the stranger's JavaScript, but TestClient, curl, and any script read it fine. CORS stops other websites from reading responses inside a visitor's browser. Anything private still needs the token and ownership checks.

m7-l1.html:
What you'll learn

  • Trace a request through the browser, the API, and the database, and name the layer each error comes from.
  • Open and close a SQLite connection per request with a yield dependency.
  • Turn missing rows, duplicate data, and bugs into 404, 409, and 500 responses.
  • Handle fetch responses so the page shows the server's real error message.
  • Explain why serving the page from the API avoids CORS entirely.

A student leaves the title box empty and clicks Save. The page says "Saved!" The API had answered 422 with a clear message about the empty title, the database never saw a thing, and the student walks away thinking their note exists.

Nothing crashed. Each piece did its job alone: the API validated, the database stayed consistent, and the page ran its code. They just didn't pass the failure along to each other. Making a full application means deciding, for every kind of failure, who notices it, what status code it becomes, and what the person at the keyboard sees.

#One click, three programs

Read it as three conversations. The page talks HTTP to the API. The API talks SQL to the database. And the page talks to a human. A failure in the middle is only useful if it's translated at each boundary: from a Python exception into a status code and JSON, then from JSON into a sentence on screen.

#A dependency opens one connection per request

In the SQL module you opened one connection and kept it. A web server handles many requests, sometimes at the same moment on different threads, so the usual pattern is a fresh connection per request, closed when the response is done. A FastAPI dependency written with yield does exactly this: code before yield runs before the route, and the finally block runs after the response, even if the route raised.

The prints show the order: open, route, close, on every request, including the one that failed with 409. Three details in get_db are easy to miss:

  • check_same_thread=False. FastAPI may run the dependency and the route on different worker threads, and Python's sqlite3 refuses by default to use a connection from a thread that didn't create it. Since each connection belongs to one request, sharing it within that request is safe.
  • row_factory = sqlite3.Row, so dict(row) gives JSON-ready dictionaries.
  • PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON, because it's per connection, and this is now where every connection is born.

A dependency also makes testing easier. app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = some_other_function swaps in a different database for a test run without touching the routes, which you'll do in the build.

#Turn failures into the right status code

Every failure should end up as a status code the client can act on and a detail message a person can read. Most of the mapping is a habit:

What went wrong Who notices Status Example detail
Body or parameter breaks the model Pydantic, before your code 422 a list of field errors
No token, or a bad one your auth dependency 401 "Missing or invalid token"
Not the owner your route 403 "You can only change your own notes"
No such row your route, after a SELECT 404 "No member with that id"
UNIQUE or other constraint fails SQLite, as IntegrityError 409 "A member with that email already exists"
A bug: typo in SQL, None where a row was expected nobody, until it crashes 500 "Internal Server Error"

The last row is special. An uncaught exception becomes a plain-text 500 Internal Server Error, and the full traceback goes to the server's terminal, not to the client. That's the right default: a traceback tells an attacker which tables and files you have. Your job is to make 500s rare, not to make them chatty.

⚠️ Watch out

Catching too much. except Exception: raise HTTPException(400, "Bad request") around a route hides real bugs as the client's fault, and you'll never see the traceback. Catch the specific exception you expect (sqlite3.IntegrityError) and let surprises become 500s you can find in the server log.

#fetch resolves even when the server says no

This is the bug from the start. fetch only rejects its promise when the request couldn't be made at all, such as the server being down or the network being off. A 404, 409, 422, or 500 is a perfectly successful delivery of bad news, so the code after await fetch(...) runs either way. You have to look at response.ok (true for 200 to 299) yourself.

The program below runs in Node. A fake fetch at the top stands in for the server and answers the way FastAPI does, including the plain-text 500, which is not JSON.

The naive version says "Saved!" three times. The careful api helper does three things: checks response.ok, reads JSON only when the response says it is JSON (calling .json() on "Internal Server Error" would throw a confusing SyntaxError), and turns FastAPI's two detail shapes, a string or a list of field errors, into one readable sentence. Every call in the page goes through this one function, so no button can forget the check.

#Serve the page from the API, and CORS goes away

If the page lives at http://127.0.0.1:5500 (say, from a live-preview extension) and the API at http://127.0.0.1:8000, the ports differ, so they are different origins and the browser applies CORS. The simplest fix is to not have two origins: let FastAPI serve the HTML file too.

Now the page calls fetch("/api/notes") with a path and no host, the browser sends it to the same origin it loaded the page from, and there's no CORS to configure. Putting every API route under /api keeps them clearly apart from page files. (check_dir=False only lets this snippet start without a static folder; leave it out in your project so a missing folder is reported right away.)

Check your understanding

4 questions

1The API returns 409 with {"detail": "A member with that email already exists"}. What does await fetch(...) do?

  • fetch only rejects when no response arrives at all. A 409 is a response.

  • Your code has to check ok and read the detail itself.

  • fetch doesn't retry anything on its own; your code decides what happens next.

Show answer

B. Your code has to check ok and read the detail itself.

2Why does get_db use yield inside try/finally instead of return conn?

  • Plain return dependencies are common; they just can't clean up afterwards.

  • Code after yield runs once the request is finished, and finally makes it run on errors too.

  • It changes when cleanup happens, not how fast SQL runs.

Show answer

B. Code after yield runs once the request is finished, and finally makes it run on errors too.

3A route has a typo, SELECT * FROM memberz. What does the client receive?

  • 404 is for a resource the client asked about. This is a server bug.

  • 422 means the client's input was invalid; the client did nothing wrong here.

  • Uncaught exceptions become a 500, and the details stay on the server.

Show answer

C. Uncaught exceptions become a 500, and the details stay on the server.

4The page is served by FastAPI at http://127.0.0.1:8000/ and calls fetch("/api/notes"). Do you need CORSMiddleware?

  • Same scheme, host, and port, so the browser applies no cross-origin rules.

  • CORS only applies when the page's origin differs from the API's.

  • Method doesn't matter when the origin is the same.

Show answer

A. Same scheme, host, and port, so the browser applies no cross-origin rules.

Key takeaways

  • Every failure should cross each boundary as something the next layer understands: exception, then status and detail, then a sentence on screen.
  • Use a yield dependency to open one SQLite connection per request and close it in finally; add check_same_thread=False.
  • Catch the exceptions you expect (IntegrityError becomes 409, a missing row becomes 404) and let real bugs become logged 500s.
  • fetch resolves on 4xx and 5xx. Check response.ok, parse JSON only when it is JSON, and show detail.
  • Serving the page and the API from one FastAPI app means one origin and no CORS setup.

#Further reading

  • FastAPI: dependencies with yield (opens in a new tab) explains exactly when the code after yield runs, including with exceptions.
  • FastAPI: handling errors (opens in a new tab) covers HTTPException, custom exception handlers, and overriding the 422 format.
  • MDN: using the Fetch API (opens in a new tab), including the section on checking that a response was successful.

What you'll learn

  • Back every notes route with parameterized SQL through a get_db dependency.
  • Write a partial update with COALESCE instead of building SQL strings.
  • Point tests at their own database with app.dependency_overrides.
  • Build a page that lists, creates, and deletes notes with fetch, and shows the API's error messages.
  • Serve the page from FastAPI and know the trade-offs of free hosting for a SQLite app.

This is the module where the pieces meet. By the end you'll have one folder that runs as a complete app: open http://127.0.0.1:8000, type a note, and it's saved in a database file that survives restarts. Leave the title empty and the page shows the API's own message instead of a fake "Saved!".

Here is the page you're building. It's live: try saving a note with an empty title, then a real one, then delete it. On this lesson page a small pretend server stands in for FastAPI (the first <script> block); everything below it is the real file.

Your project folder will look like this. The cells below share one Python session, the way a notebook does. Steps 1 and 2 are the start of main.py, step 3 is test_main.py, and the complete main.py comes at the end.

#Step 1: The schema and the connection dependency

init_db takes a path so tests can make their own database. get_db is the per-request connection from the Notes lesson.

SQLite's datetime('now') is in UTC, written as YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS. Text in that format sorts correctly, which the list route relies on.

#Step 2: Routes backed by SQL

The paths move under /api (/api/notes instead of the earlier /notes), so they can never collide with page files once FastAPI serves the page too. Each route asks for db and runs one or two parameterized statements. find_note raises the 404 in one place. The PATCH route updates only the fields the client sent: a missing field arrives as None, and COALESCE(?, title) means "use the new value, or keep the old one if the new one is NULL". That keeps the SQL fixed, with no string-building.

create_note reads the row back with find_note instead of echoing the input, so the response includes the id and created_at that only the database knows. The with db: blocks commit each write, which matters now: forget the commit and the next request, on a fresh connection, wouldn't see the note.

#Step 3: Tests on their own database

Tests that create and delete notes shouldn't touch notes.db, where your real notes live. app.dependency_overrides tells FastAPI "whenever a route asks for get_db, call this instead", so every route gets a connection to test_notes.db without changing a line of them. setUp rebuilds that file before each test.

The last line is the proof: the note from step 2 is still the only row in the real file. "First" and "Second" both get created_at in the same second, which is why the list route also sorts by id DESC as a tie-breaker; without it, test_create_then_list_newest_first could pass or fail depending on timing.

#Step 4: The page

Save the page from the top of this lesson as static/index.html, without the preview-only <script> block. Three choices in it are worth copying into every front end you write:

  1. One api() function does every request, so the response.ok check, the JSON check, and the error message format happen in one place.
  2. Paths, not full URLs. fetch("/api/notes") goes to whatever origin served the page, so the same file works on your laptop and on a host.
  3. textContent, never innerHTML, for user data. A note titled <img src=x onerror=alert(1)> would run that script if inserted as HTML. With textContent it's just odd text.

The title box has maxlength but not required. Normally you'd add required for a friendlier form; it's left off so you can watch the server's 422 arrive. Browser checks are a convenience for honest users; the server's checks are the ones that count, because anyone can send a request without your page.

#Step 5: Serve the page and run everything

Here is the finished main.py. Compared with the steps, it adds the StaticFiles mount at the bottom and finds notes.db and static/ next to the file, so it works from any folder you start it in.

From the notes-api folder, start it and open the page:

Go to http://127.0.0.1:8000. To watch the conversation, open your browser's developer tools (F12, or Cmd+Option+I on a Mac) and choose the Network tab, then save a note. You'll see the POST /api/notes request, its 201 or 422 status, and the exact JSON, the same thing your tests check. http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs still works too, because /docs is registered before the mount.

#Step 6: Putting it online for free

Hosting changes often, so check each provider's current docs before you rely on these details. The big question for this app is where notes.db lives, because many free plans throw away files.

  • Render (free web service): connect a GitHub repository, set the build command to pip install -r requirements.txt and the start command to uvicorn main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port $PORT. A free service sleeps after 15 minutes without traffic and takes about a minute to wake. Its filesystem is temporary, so notes.db is wiped on every redeploy, restart, or spin-down. That's fine for showing the app off; for data you want to keep, you'd use a hosted database instead (Render's free Postgres databases expire after 30 days).
  • PythonAnywhere: your files stay put, so a SQLite file survives. Its support for FastAPI (an ASGI app) is a beta feature that you set up with their pa command-line tool, following their "ASGI" help pages; check there for what a free account currently includes.

For either one, make a requirements.txt next to main.py containing the line fastapi[standard], which pulls in Uvicorn too. And never deploy with secrets in your code; read them from environment variables, which every host lets you set.

Check your understanding

3 questions

1Why does the StaticFiles mount come after all the @app routes?

  • Python doesn't care. FastAPI checks routes and mounts in the order they were added.

  • Registering the API routes first means /api/notes and /docs win, and everything else falls through to the files.

  • It only reads files from the static folder.

Show answer

B. Registering the API routes first means /api/notes and /docs win, and everything else falls through to the files.

2Why do the tests use app.dependency_overrides[get_db] instead of changing DB_PATH?

  • Routes ask for get_db; the override answers with a test connection instead.

  • It could be reassigned, but every function would then depend on the order things were imported and set, which is easy to get wrong.

  • They don't affect how tests are scheduled.

Show answer

A. Routes ask for get_db; the override answers with a test connection instead.

3A note's title is <b>hi</b>. What does the page show?

  • That would only happen with innerHTML, which this page never uses for note data.

  • textContent puts characters on screen as text, so markup in user data can't run.

  • The model allows any characters. Safety comes from how the page displays them.

Show answer

B. textContent puts characters on screen as text, so markup in user data can't run.

Key takeaways

  • Every route gets its connection from get_db, runs parameterized SQL, and commits with with db:.
  • COALESCE(?, column) gives you a partial update with fixed SQL.
  • app.dependency_overrides points tests at their own database file, rebuilt before each test.
  • The page's single api() helper checks response.ok, parses only real JSON, and shows detail.
  • Mount StaticFiles last so the page and the API share one origin, with no CORS needed.
  • On free hosts with temporary disks, a SQLite file resets on every restart. Pick hosting knowing where your data lives.

  • Add an Edit button that turns a note into inputs and sends PATCH with only the fields that changed.
  • Add GET /api/notes?q=word that filters with LIKE '%' || ? || '%', and a search box that calls it as you type.
  • Bring back the accounts from Module 6: a users table, a tokens table, and an Authorization header sent by api(). The capstone starter does exactly this.
